#156584. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.
  • This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s upcoming monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.
  • Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s upcoming monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

Recent findings suggest that the time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and stated the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and latest ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb aims to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the firm said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment complications, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”.

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the organization’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Recent findings suggest that preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

Industry observers note that “Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”.

Recent findings suggest that for agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

Industry News: 5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar.
  • In a recent development, what if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth?
  • It has been revealed that those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

In a recent development, what if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

It has been revealed that those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a manufacturer bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a substantial business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

According to recent reports, to that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

The tech giant recently revealed $73.5 million in new funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

In a recent development, the idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness company recently revealed a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

Industry observers note that intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

In a recent development, the organization markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It claims it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

In a recent development, intake intends to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

Industry observers note that its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data highlights.

Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026.

Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

In a recent development, trashLab claims its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

Recent findings suggest that the firm notes hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026.

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a new kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

According to recent reports, its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get new production lines up and running.

The startup states it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

The investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026.

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

According to recent reports, the Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The manufacturer describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

Industry observers note that customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite launched in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed indicates its newly introduced funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

It has been revealed that tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data shows.

Related Crunchbase query: Space And Satellite Tech Startup Funding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:53 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly briefed Congressional staffers about Alice Huang, the cloud executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy.

The classified discussion took place on Tuesday, sources told the Fresh York Times and the Wall Street Journal today. It was attended by staff members of the House and Senate intelligence committees. The briefing is said to have included representatives of the FBI, CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

In a recent development, alice Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud provider that has reportedly bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Corp. chips. The company is under investigation for allegedly breaching U.S. export controls. Those controls prohibit companies from selling cutting-edge artificial intelligence chips to customers in China.

On Oct. 29, the Times revealed that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang. The paper stated that she had been “found to be passing intelligence” to China. A few days later, other outlets reported that U.S. officials had not yet concluded that Alice Huang is a spy. The U.S. Justice Department reaffirmed that’s the case shortly thereafter.

According to the Times, this week’s classified Congressional briefing included a summary of the information that U.S. intelligence agencies have collected about Alice Huang. Those agencies’ representatives reportedly “did not dispute” that she had gathered information for China. However, they stated that there’s no evidence China’s MSS spy agency directed her to initiate the affair.

Industry observers note that some U.S. officials reportedly believe Alice Huang can still be considered a spy. Others are said to see her ties to the country’s intelligence service as ”more circumstantial.” According to the Journal, officials don’t believe that Alice Huang passed any “intelligence of significance” to China.

According to recent reports, the briefers reportedly told Congressional staffers that Kang Wei, a businessman believed to be Huang’s husband, is a “more significant” figure. They stated that Kang is a Chinese intelligence asset who was “often” in touch with the country’s spy agency.

On Nov. 12, the Journal reported that Kang had known Jensen Huang for over a decade. The publication later revealed that he had built a data center network in China.

The briefing reportedly did not cover the most sensitive information the U.S. intelligence community has gathered about Alice Huang. Additionally, it didn’t include a classified memo about her relationship with Jensen Huang that was drafted under the supervision of U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio. Congressional staffers requested a copy of the memo.

Jensen Huang is set to appear before three House committees on Dec. 1. Prior to the spy controversy, he was reportedly scheduled to make a product announcement that day. The closed-door briefing will be followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

A ‘Holiday Hangover’: How Black Friday and Holiday Shopping Can Delay Your Mortgage Next Year

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the holiday season is finally here.
  • Otherwise, it could derail your approval for a mortgage and delay your homeownership goals.
  • While Black Friday sales, Cyber Monday deals, and holiday splurges may be tempting, making larger purchases or taking on additional debt could easily create unexpected issues with your mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the holiday season is finally here. And if you’re planning to close on a home in late 2026 or early 2027, you should be extra cautious of your holiday spending.

Otherwise, it could derail your approval for a mortgage and delay your homeownership goals.

While Black Friday sales, Cyber Monday deals, and holiday splurges may be tempting, making larger purchases or taking on additional debt could easily create unexpected issues with your mortgage.

According to recent reports, before loading up your shopping cart, consider what the data notes about this year’s holiday spending. According to the National Retail Foundation, U.S. holiday retail sales will hit $1.013 trillion in November and December 2026—a 4.2% hike over 2025.

Furthermore, an estimated 182.7 million Americans proposal to shop during Thanksgiving weekend alone, with Black Friday expected to attract an additional 126 million.

Industry observers note that the high spending projections come at a time when credit card debt is already out of control. The Federal Reserve Bank of Newly introduced York found that Americans carried approximately $1.285 trillion in credit card debt as of the third quarter of 2026, an increase of $52 billion compared with the same time last year.

Industry observers note that “Be frugal now. Once you’ve moved into the house and have rebuilt a cash cushion, you can splurge on gifts. Or maybe you’ll realize you’d rather devote the extra cash to renovating the kitchen,” says Jeff Ostrowski, housing marketing analyst at Bankrate.

By being mindful of your purchases, you could enjoy the holiday season without jeopardizing your future home.

It has been revealed that before you close on a mortgage, all lenders will pull your credit history. By doing so, they can determine if you’ve opened any new accounts or initiated any new inquiries since you were initially approved.

“Simply opening a credit card at checkout for 20% savings will result in a new inquiry, account, and monthly payment. While this will only negatively affect your score slightly, the underwriter may require an explanation letter. It may also result in a higher rate if your score drops significantly,” explains Ali Zane, CEO and personal finance expert at IMAX Credit Repair in Los Angeles.

Zane points out that many buy now, pay later programs, which are popular during the holiday shopping season, also report to the credit bureaus.

Recent findings suggest that “Each one you agree to will lead to another monthly payment. And unfortunately, purchasing an item you’ll pay off over four installments can significantly affect your debt-to-income (DTI) ratio, especially if you're already at the maximum amount, which is usually 45%, depending on the lender,” says Zane.

Credit card balances, which affect your DTI ratio, will likely have the most significant effect on your mortgage approval, particularly when increased spending raises your credit utilization and monthly debt obligations.

“If you go on a holiday spending spree and raise your utilization from 8% to 60%, you may see a significant decrease in your score as well as an increase in your DTI,” says Zane.

Cash reserves are also important to most lenders.

“An underwriter will want to verify you have sufficient amounts for the down payment, closing cost, and reserves. You don't want to spend this amount of money on furniture, appliances, and holiday gifts,” Zane cautions.

The holidays are a great time to score great deals, but these deals can easily put your home purchase at risk.

Sources indicate that “Many stores, both online and in person, will offer incentives to get you to buy right there and now. Sometimes, it's a massive discount and other times it's a rebate they'll give back to you. In any case, if you’re in the middle of buying a home, think twice before pursuing them,” claims Ray Hicks, home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage in Brentwood, TN.

Recent findings suggest that hicks cites a sitution that he sees often: You’re in the middle of the mortgage process. Then, your car breaks down or the dealership has some crazy New Year’s deal on a car you can't refuse, so you go for it. Your monthly payment on the shiny new toy puts you over the maximum DTI and you eventually learn you can't buy a home after all.

Here’s the moral of the story: To be as safe as possible this holiday season and ensure your home purchase goes through as planned, make only those purchases you can cover with your debit card or cash on hand.

“Normal expenses like groceries and gifts that fit in your budget are fine. New lines of credit and debt are usually not,” explains Zane.

Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun stated mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

Industry observers note that “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant stated she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

In a recent development, “There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant stated in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant mentioned. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

Industry observers note that as a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he noted. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

Sources indicate that “If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun mentioned in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale noted existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

In a recent development, “Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she mentioned. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale remarked jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

In a recent development, “[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun stated rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

Sources indicate that “One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he mentioned. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

It has been revealed that however, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.

Sources indicate that chip had unilaterally decided to purchase the outdated manse three years ago. Once he realized the palatial investment property had more problems than anticipated, he turned to Joanna for help transforming the space. Adding to the pressure was a three-month timeline to transform the place.

In an exclusive clip shared with Realtor.com from the back-to-back premiere episodes, the Gainses hold a pre-renovation open house with two of their designer friends to get a fresh perspective and some professional guidance on what changes are necessary.

The four experts gather in the mansion’s oversized living room that Jo previously described as something out of “Beauty and the Beast” due to the high ceiling, multiple decorative columns, and golden paint covering the walls. The room is anchored by honey-toned hardwood floors and adorned with elaborate trim, molding, and millwork throughout.

Standing in front of a cream-colored fireplace with a sprawling floral arrangement on its mantel, Chip asks the women what task they want him to tackle.

“What curtains would you like me to demo?” he inquires.

When one of the designers comments that Chip “needs a man job” to do, he signals he’s totally up for the challenge.

“A man job. A real man,” notes Chip.

Joanna explains that “they really want to see the room without curtains,” so Chip makes his way toward a wall of windows and French doors that are concealed by a peachy-orange, grid-patterned window covering lined with pom-poms and tassels.

As the impromptu demo day begins to unfold, Jo nervously places her hands on her head while Chip confidently tugs on one side of the curtain.

It has been revealed that “This is turning into a ‘Saturday Night Live’ skit,” Joanna states. “I’m sweating.”.

“I feel like this is going to be totally doable,” Chips responds.

Sources indicate that chip’s prediction is correct. The curtain comes down easily, so Joanna praises her husband and directs him to continue.

According to recent reports, “My hero! OK, do the other thing,” she says.

Chip proceeds, but he quickly discovers the second side requires a bigger effort to bring down the drapery due to the metal track that held up the coverings in the first place.

It has been revealed that “Oh, God. There was a little more to that one,” admits Chip.

Jo and the designer guests are pleased with what’s exposed. Natural light pours into the large living space from the glass doors and windows that now clearly have a view of the property’s mature trees and a covered patio built with beautiful red brick.

Sources indicate that “Yes, I’m feeling it. Pretty awesome,” the designers say.

In a recent development, typically, it’s Chip who often displays his silly side on work sites, while Jo plays the part of his professional-minded foil. However, pleased with the results of the curtain reveal, a noticeably relieved Joanna momentarily pivots from interior design to fashion design.

Industry observers note that “Style me. I want a dress,” she notes as she wraps herself up in the downed curtains with an assist from Chip.

Sources indicate that “Well, twist. Turn, turn, turn. There you go. Now that’s it. Yeah, just that. Wow,” he comments when he sees the finished frock on his wife.

In a recent development, “Very Italian. That’s cool. Pretty awesome,” notes the admiring group.

After Jo models her fresh look, more of the mansion’s ground floor is visible. Just past the double glass door entrance of the home, a staircase with an ornate wrought-iron railing leads to the second floor, and a black table fills space in the grand foyer.

Behind Jo, a rendering of her vision for the room demonstrates the area styled with an oversized mirror above the fireplace and several comfy chairs placed opposite a couch. With that strategy in place, she lays out the next steps for the rest of the residence.

“So I think at this point, it’s mainly the kitchen, and then it’s just a refresh,” states Joanna.

The pair of experts agree and reassure the Gainses that a less is more approach is the way to go.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KeyBank shares warning signs and practical steps for avoiding phishing, fake shopping sites, payment app scams and other holiday fraud.

Sources indicate that CLEVELAND, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As holiday shopping picks up, so do opportunities for scammers.

Consumers shopping online, tracking packages, buying gift cards or donating to charities can encounter increasingly convincing fraud attempts. Scammers are also using artificial intelligence to create fake retail websites, emails, text messages and even AI-generated voices designed to impersonate trusted companies or people.

Knowing what to look for can help consumers recognize potential fraud before they share personal information or send money.

What are the most common holiday shopping scams?

Here are several scams consumers should watch for during the holiday season:.

Bank imposter scams. Fraudsters may call, text or email pretending to represent a consumer's bank. They may claim there has been a suspicious transaction or login attempt, then ask for a one-time passcode, login credentials or debit card information. KeyBank will not initiate a call or text asking for your online banking username or password. KeyBank also will not ask a client to send money to themselves using ZelleÂ®, an account transfer or a wire payment, or request remote access to your computer or mobile device. However, in some cases, we will call to verify your identity by asking for a one-time passcode that is sent to your mobile device.

Phishing and smishing scams. Fraudulent emails and text messages can look like legitimate communications from retailers, banks or delivery companies. Scammers may also use AI to create convincing fake retail websites and communications intended to capture debit card, credit card or other personal information. A common example is a fake package-delivery message asking for payment to release or redeliver an order.

Vishing and AI voice scams. Criminals can use AI-generated voices in phone calls to impersonate customer service representatives, delivery companies, family members or others in an effort to obtain sensitive information.

Recent findings suggest that payment app scams. Consumers should be cautious when an unfamiliar seller asks for payment through ZelleÂ®, Venmo, Cash App, wire transfer or cryptocurrency. Recovering money sent to a fraudulent seller through these methods can be difficult.

Recent findings suggest that online marketplace scams. Fraudsters may advertise popular holiday gifts at unusually low prices, then request advance payment through a payment app, gift card or cryptocurrency before disappearing.

Gift card scams. Criminals may tamper with gift cards displayed on retail racks or convince victims to provide gift card numbers over the phone to make supposedly urgent payments.

Elon Musk has reacted to a post by Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ), in which the latter shared that he used Grok Bot to tidy up his X following list.

Sources indicate that according to CZ, the bot was tasked with removing inactive and abusive accounts from the list of people he follows, though accounts with constructive criticism were supposed to stay. CZ was not fully sure about the results, adding "AI did it" with a shrug emoji.

Musk replied with "Cool." Later, CZ added in the same thread that it "worked well so far.".

According to recent reports, back in September, CZ had to address rumors about his account being hacked after users noticed that he had unfollowed a number of profiles. Per CZ, at that time he removed accounts that were inactive for more than 30 days.

Since then, the product has received praise from Nvidia head Jensen Huang, who said in October that Grok Bot usage was "really skyrocketing." Musk himself claimed on SpaceX's Q3 earnings call that he had never seen a product grow this fast.

It has been revealed that on Coinbase, Grok was responsible for 59.54% of AI-agent trading volume from Sept. 14 to Sept. 21. For comparison, Claude had 13.37% and ChatGPT only 1.54%. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong then named Grok the leading client for agentic traders on the platform, to which Musk also responded with "Cool.".

According to recent reports, at the same time, there were complaints. NewCore researchers reported last week that Grok Bot made 31 unrequested access attempts to email, calendar, Slack and GitHub accounts on two employee laptops within five days, ignoring the command to stop.

In a recent development, it was only last month that Musk was trolling Binance after the exchange lost about $6.3 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, the largest one in crypto history so far. Among other things, Musk posted "Everyday is Zeroday" and replied with fire and laughing emojis to CZ's earlier warning about phishing links.

CZ then asked Musk to stop, calling it a "bad time to troll," and reminded him that Binance's $500 million investment in Twitter in 2022 has become a stake in SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.

Now, the two seem to be on good terms again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

It has been revealed that on this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking significant risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy indicates many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

Sources indicate that for agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mediwhale, an AI healthcare company that uses noninvasive retinal imaging to assess the risk of cardiometabolic diseases, today confirmed that it has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for Dr. Noon CVD, its retinal-AI cardiovascular risk assessment software. The clearance paves the way for Mediwhale to introduce Dr. Noon CVD into U.S. clinical practice.

Dr. Noon CVD combines AI analysis of retinal images with age and sex to estimate an individual's 10-year risk of a first atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Results classify patients into one of three risk categories to support clinicians' cardiovascular risk assessment alongside other clinical information.[1].

Cardiovascular prevention in the United States is placing greater emphasis on earlier intervention informed by individualized risk assessment, as reflected in the 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline on the management of dyslipidemia.[2] Mediwhale aims to contribute to this approach by offering clinicians a noninvasive way to assess cardiovascular risk through retinal imaging.

"Retinal cameras are already in primary care clinics across the United States, where they are used every day for diabetic eye exams," stated Kevin Taegeun Choi, CEO of Mediwhale. "With FDA clearance, that same retinal exam can now do more: support cardiovascular risk assessment. We intend to be first to bring this to U.S. primary care, working with partners that already operate these networks and building U.S. real-world data as we go.".

Mediwhale is an AI healthcare organization that uses noninvasive retinal imaging to assess cardiometabolic disease risk. In the United States, Dr. Noon CVD is FDA-cleared software for cardiovascular risk assessment. For more information, visit https://mediwhale.com/.

Industry observers note that on Zcash Community Forum, a latest grant application has emerged which is aimed at making Zcash even more private on iPhone-based wallets. The author seeks a $25,000 grant in order to implement a private way of retrieving encrypted transaction memos.

According to recent reports, essentially, the proposal allows hiding which transactions people have been looking up, which is a potential deanonymization vector. Considering how Zcash placese itself on the market, revealing any kind of external information is a step which might shorten the distance between a random transaction and a specific user.

The proposal itself won't touch the network or the blockchain behind it as is. It's an improvement of an SDK (Software Development Kit) that will allow developers to use tools that can help make Zcash more privacy-resilient.

Zcash transactions today contain encrypted data called memos. Various wallets read those memos in order to receive information about the transaction. The message itself stays encrypted, so is retrieved data, however, the query itself is not protected by any means which enables potential tracing.

Even when using Tor, the transaction ID stay out in the open and can be read by anyone.

With the integration of private information retrieval into SDK, hiding the query itself wil be easier, messages would be decrypted locally and wallets themselves will verify the returned information.

Recent findings suggest that the first tests have already shown promising results. During testing in an iOS Simulator, the modified SDK managed to retrieve a 512-byte memo through an encrypted query, without revealing the transaction ID to the wallet server.

The developer expects the implementation of the proposal by January 30, 2027, with testing on physical iPhones and a public SDK release planned for the final stage.

However, the proposal is still seeking funding, and its actual adoption will depend on individual wallet developers.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

In a recent development, ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in Fresh York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

Recent findings suggest that that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an crucial question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Sources indicate that today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

It has been revealed that the mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

Sources indicate that when a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

It has been revealed that A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

Sources indicate that at The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Sources indicate that invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

According to recent reports, david Schwartz, CTO Emeritus at Ripple and one of the creators of the XRP Ledger, has once again commented on his XRP and Bitcoin sales. This time, the reason was a viral post on X that claimed he had sold almost all of his crypto over the last few months.

Recent findings suggest that according to the post, Schwartz's portfolio reportedly went from 26 million XRP, 1,500 BTC and 40,000 ETH to just 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH. The author called it "an insane reduction" and also referred to Schwartz as the current CTO of Ripple, while he now holds the emeritus title.

In a recent development, schwartz replied that the timeline in the post was wrong. "That wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade," he wrote. As proof, he shared his own post from April 21, 2019. In that post, Schwartz noted he was still sticking to the "de-risking strategy" that he and his wife agreed on when they first decided to put their own money into crypto. He also admitted back then that selling during the bull run "still hurt.".

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, Schwartz did not dispute the numbers themselves. "But it's basically true. I hate risk. I can't help it," he wrote in a follow-up post. According to him, pretty much every big risk he has ever taken has worked out well, and rationally he should be taking more risk as he gets wealthier. "But I hate it. I just hate risk and can't do anything about it," Schwartz added.

That wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade. You can find me talking about this in many posts over the years, like this one:https://t.co/5MgcPZ5qyG.

At press time, XRP was trading at around $0.939, Bitcoin at $61,477 and Ethereum at $1,722. At these prices, the remaining 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH are worth about $2.89 million, and XRP accounts for more than 97% of this sum.

For comparison, at current prices, the peak holdings mentioned in the post would be worth over $185 million, with Bitcoin alone accounting for about half of it.

Schwartz has already explained his sales several times this year. In May, he stated he did not have much XRP left and had tried to move most of his assets, other than Ripple stock, away from crypto exposure. In July, he said he regrets selling XRP at $0.10 and ETH at around $1, but noted that he and his wife had agreed to sell at every newly introduced all-time high.

Earlier in November, Schwartz disclosed that he sold about 2.5 million XRP in 2025. Per Schwartz, most of these tokens were received in 2020 and 2023, and he paid approximately $1.7 million in capital gains tax on those sales. He shared this in response to a user who called XRP a "terrible investment.".

Among other things, Schwartz has previously stated that his main exposure to the crypto sector now comes through Ripple stock, not XRP. In March, Ripple introduced a share buyback of up to $750 million that valued the company at $50 billion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the October jobs report demonstrated employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

In a recent development, the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

In a recent development, at October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

Industry observers note that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh mentioned in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Recent findings suggest that adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

It has been revealed that existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Sources indicate that forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

Sources indicate that the October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

Cardano just saw a death cross on its daily chart, with the 50 MA falling below the 200 MA. The timing of this signal remains significant, as it marks the second consecutive November in the last two years that Cardano has marked a death cross. Cardano saw a death cross in November 2025, and the same is happening this November.

In a recent development, the signal in November 2025 was followed by months of falling prices, which has led some to speculate that the cryptocurrency may have further downside or a recovery ahead of the end of 2026. The current uncertainty in the market has added to concerns. A volatile weekend saw Cardano fall as low as $0.134, its weakest level since December 2020, before rebounding. This recovery has entered its third day, with ADA up 2.05% in the last 24 hours to $0.146.

In a recent development, whether that rebound holds is the test traders will keep an eye on. The $0.18 area represents an initial resistance level, while a stronger recovery toward the $0.198 to $0.20 range would bring Cardano closer to its daily moving averages.

Another possibility is sideways trading as ADA attempts to establish a sustainable bottom. Its daily RSI is flirting with oversold territory that may trigger a relief bounce, but that’s not enough to confirm a trend reversal. In a bearish scenario, continued selling pressure could push ADA below its recent $0.134 support area, exposing lower price levels.

Industry observers note that crypto markets head into a holiday-shortened U.S. week with inflation data that could shape how big a rate increase the Federal Reserve will consider next month. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, is due Wednesday and is expected to show prices rose 0.3% in October after a 0.5% gain in September.

Five different node implementations have now produced blocks on Cardano mainnet. Protocol version 12 testing continues on Musashi and Dijkstra (11.2.1 Pre-release) testnets.

Work progresses on a node version 11.2.x with Mainnet clearance; until then, 11.1.3 remains the recommended version. Node 11.2.0 introduced a latest “envelope” config file format, which will be the format published on the config file pages for networks running 11.2.0 and above.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“It’s my job to put New York families first,” remarked Hochul, who explained as a mother and grandmother the matter is “deeply personal.” Hochul added that some of the wayward toys on the market at the moment have engaged children in “inappropriate conversations,” while some may also manipulate a child’s feelings or put their privacy at risk.

Industry observers note that “This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” the governor mentioned. “When tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to our kids and our babies, you bet I’m going to have something to say about it.”.

Industry observers note that though dangerous dolls manipulating innocent children may sound like the plot of Hollywood movie, recent tests of certain chatbot-powered toys have become a real cause for concern. When journalists at NBC News tested the Pixie Paw, an AI-powered plush cat toy marketed to children aged three and older, it reportedly shared stories of massacres, gang rape and firing squads in what was described as graphic detail.

Other tests have shown some of the toys can become very convincing when trying to persuade the young user that they are human. “Parents have enough to worry about,” said Hochul, who was also aware some of the smart toys have encouraged kids to jump out of windows.

In a recent development, state senator Andrew Gounardes applauded the move, saying that modern life seems to be mimicking science fiction of days gone by. He invoked an episode of the “Twilight Zone that featured the Talky Tina doll, an insidious, possessed toy that tried to persuade a young girl to murder her strict stepfather.

New York Attorney General Letitia James explained that the toys being put on the market is reckless when they clearly expose “young people to inappropriate content and put “their mental health at risk.” She added, “We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of massive tech.”.

Hochul has been vocal about the dangers of AI for some time, recently imposing the first statewide moratorium on fresh data centers and last month signing a bill titled “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors,” which will prohibit firms from developing chatbots that feature elements that could be harmful to minors.

#156560. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1072 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • In a recent development, access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

In a recent development, access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely indicates you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

Recent findings suggest that this fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s revision calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the tech giant can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same tech giant that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

Sources indicate that in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

Industry observers note that if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

According to recent reports, how to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

According to recent reports, now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

It has been revealed that how to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The tech giant running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

According to recent reports, how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

Sources indicate that how to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Sources indicate that amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bronwyn Newport has a new Utah home—and she just gave fans and her estranged husband a tour of the dwelling.

On the Nov. 25 episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” the fashion blogger received a visit from Todd Bradley, her estranged husband. The couple declared their separation in December 2025 after nine years of marriage.

The tech investor initially mentioned he “just wanted to come by and see” Newport and her fresh home, but soon admitted that he had stopped by to apologize after an explosive conversation the pair had shared over dinner in the previous episode.

"It's time to move on," Bradley noted.

In a confessional interview, Newport admitted that Bradley had reached out to smooth things over after their last dramatic conversation, but that she had not yet been ready to talk.

Instead, she extended an invitation to her newly introduced property.

“I invited him to the house because it’s a smaller, nicer way for me to say, ‘This is what I’m doing, and this is the direction I’m going,’ without saying things that are hard for him to hear,” she explained.

Bradley had not yet seen the home in person, although he remarked it looked nice in the photographs he had looked at. Newport offered him a tour of “some of it.”.

“The whole basement is going to be Gwen and Logan’s domain,” she explained, referring to her 20-year-old daughter and her daughter’s boyfriend.

In a recent development, the ground level of the home—which was empty at the time of the impromptu tour—featured hardwood flooring, an open-concept plan, a fireplace, and plenty of windows. There were also recessed lights and a glass sliding door, which led to an outdoor space.

“Upstairs is really Muzzy’s space,” Newport stated as she walked up the steps of the yet-to-be-furnished home with Bradley.

She said that the upstairs space—in which her mother, who goes by Muzzy, will reside in—includes a kitchen and essentially functions as an apartment.

Finally, Newport brought Bradley into her primary squite, a light-filled space lined with expansive windows. The room features an en suite bathroom with a walk-in shower and tub, which she remarked she’s very excited about, as she and Bradley had previously discussed a remodel of the home they shared, which would have included a lavish bathtub.

There’s also a well-organized walk-in closet, though fans of the show will understand that it’s likely not going to be enough space for Newport’s massive wardrobe.

In a Sept. 30 interview with Vulture, she did a photo shoot in a storage unit she has in the nearby suburb of Millcreek, UT, which serves the sole purpose of storing all of her clothes and accessories.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s very weird to give Todd a tour of a house that’s going to be mine and not his,” she said during the episode. “There is a part of me that feels I need to be totally free and separate of Todd, but there’s a part of me that is scared to death to not have Todd be a part of my life at all.”.

Sources indicate that newport and Bradley had moved into a sprawling Salt Lake City home not long before she joined the cast. In a September 2024 tour of the previous abode, she said they had been living there for a year and a half after moving from nearby Park City.

It has been revealed that in the video, Newport revealed she came across the home in a viral listing. It had originally featured a sunken floor with a "psychedelic carpet,” which she stated she “liked and really wanted to keep.”.

Per Bradley’s wishes, they upgraded the space to have sleek hardwood floors.

In a recent development, “I love a project, so I wanted this old, haunted house in Salt Lake that we could remodel,” she said. “When we first came in, I was obsessed with this living room, the view of Salt Lake and the mountains, all the light, and a big space for me to have tons of parties all of the time.”.

The home was boldly decorated, with a royal blue kitchen, rainbow couches in the living room, and a color-drenched lavender office space, with built-in shelving filled with art and designer accessories.

After their separation, Newport and Bradley sold the home for an undisclosed amount in an off-market deal.

The transaction has become a storyline this season of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City,” with friend of the cast Britani Bateman flexing her real estate expertise to suggest that the home was priced too high when it was on the market, and that Newport must not have received the 50-50 split from the sale that she had claimed to get.
