#156522. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1528 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

Recent findings suggest that none could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

According to recent reports, ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

In a recent development, “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, remarked music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

It has been revealed that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan mentioned. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Sources indicate that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

It has been revealed that “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

According to recent reports, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

In a recent development, natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

It has been revealed that “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova remarked. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and newly introduced construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Industry observers note that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova noted. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Recent findings suggest that andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

Recent findings suggest that she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he claims, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

It has been revealed that he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

Recent findings suggest that she played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Sources indicate that shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

It has been revealed that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share upcoming songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova stated she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

It has been revealed that so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova noted, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

ORANGE COUNTY, Calif., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SoCal Digital Marketing, an established SEO and digital advertising agency serving businesses throughout Southern California and nationwide, confirms the launch of its new ChatGPT Ads Management Services.

The upcoming service helps businesses explore advertising opportunities within ChatGPT through account setup, campaign strategy, ad creation, conversion tracking, and ongoing optimization.

With ChatGPT advertising continuing to expand during its beta rollout, SoCal Digital Marketing is positioning itself to help businesses evaluate this emerging channel and reach prospective customers during AI-powered research and purchasing decisions.

Bringing Real-World Advertising Experience to ChatGPT Ads.

Founded in 2012, SoCal Digital Marketing has spent more than a decade helping businesses improve their online visibility, generate qualified leads, and manage paid advertising campaigns.

The agency has already helped clients establish and manage ChatGPT advertising accounts during beta access, gaining firsthand experience with the platform's evolving campaign structure, advertising relevance signals, and management capabilities.

Founder Andrew Guida has also completed ChatGPT Ads training hosted by OpenAI, building on his experience in SEO and digital advertising dating back to 2011.

It has been revealed that "We've spent years helping businesses reach customers through Google Ads, and ChatGPT advertising represents an exciting upcoming opportunity," said Andrew Guida, founder of SoCal Digital Marketing. "What's particularly interesting is how the platform evaluates relevance. Instead of depending primarily on the exact keywords someone searches, ChatGPT Ads considers the broader context of what someone is researching and trying to accomplish.".

Industry observers note that guida added, "We've already been helping clients set up and manage accounts during beta access. That practical experience allows us to approach this new advertising channel with a better understanding of its capabilities, challenges, and opportunities.".

A Fresh Approach to Reaching Potential Customers.

Unlike traditional Google Search advertising, which relies heavily on keyword targeting, ChatGPT Ads uses conversational context and other relevance signals to help determine when sponsored advertisements may be useful.

For example, a business owner researching manufacturing services, software solutions, or professional service providers may encounter an eligible advertisement relevant to their current research.

This creates an additional opportunity for businesses to reach prospective customers while they are comparing solutions and considering their next steps.

Why Businesses Should Consider ChatGPT Advertising Early.

As a relatively newly introduced advertising platform, ChatGPT Ads may present opportunities for early adopters to begin testing campaigns before advertiser participation becomes more widespread.

While lower costs and stronger conversions are not guaranteed, businesses that begin exploring the platform can start learning which advertising messages, customer needs, and landing pages generate meaningful results.

"There's a potential advantage to learning a fresh advertising platform while it's still developing," Guida explained. "Businesses that begin testing ChatGPT Ads now can gather valuable information about customer behavior and campaign performance. The goal isn't simply to advertise somewhere new. It's to determine whether ChatGPT can become another reliable source of qualified leads.".

SoCal Digital Marketing views ChatGPT advertising as a complement to traditional SEO, Google Ads, and Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), rather than a replacement for these established marketing strategies.

The agency's expanded services are designed to help manufacturers, franchises, professional service providers, and other eligible businesses evaluate opportunities to reach customers through AI-powered advertising.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The manufacturer started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Industry observers note that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

Sources indicate that for Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

In a recent development, listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

It has been revealed that the five-year-old organization was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the firm.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the organization to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

Sources indicate that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has mentioned it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

Breaking: Why biodiversity belongs in the master plan

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking.
  • Parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment.
  • Industry observers note that pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking. Decisions about infrastructure, open space, water, landscaping and mobility made early in the planning process shape how a community functions decades later.

Parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment. But there’s growing evidence that designing those landscapes to support biodiversity can help that investment do more. Planned early as part of the infrastructure conversation, biodiversity can help a community better manage water, withstand environmental stress and create stronger connections between residents and the natural environment.

Industry observers note that pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin. Bees, butterflies and other pollinators help many flowering plants reproduce, sustaining vegetation that supports broader ecosystems.

Recent findings suggest that development decisions can remove or fragment the food sources and nesting areas those species need. At the scale of a master-planned community, developers have an opportunity to connect habitat across parks, drainage corridors and neighborhoods, making conservation part of the places people use every day.

Recent findings suggest that developers already expect infrastructure to serve a defined purpose and perform over time. Landscape systems deserve the same scrutiny.

A stormwater basin can manage runoff while also providing habitat. A trail corridor can connect residents to destinations while connecting pollinators to food and nesting resources. Plant selection can account for seasonal habitat needs alongside appearance and maintenance.

According to recent reports, these decisions are much more than aesthetic considerations. A 2024 npj Urban Sustainability review examining research across stormwater management, water purification, heat mitigation, infrastructure resilience and maintenance costs found that biodiversity can meaningfully influence how blue-green infrastructure performs. More diverse ecological systems were associated with benefits ranging from improved stormwater retention and water purification to greater resilience under changing environmental conditions.

In a recent development, for developers, the implication is practical: Ecological and engineering performance do not necessarily need to be treated as separate objectives. Incorporating habitat into drainage or open-space plans creates opportunities to serve multiple purposes within the same land area. It also brings stewardship into the budget early, when responsibilities can be assigned, and maintenance requirements can inform design.

The value of parks, trails and public spaces extends beyond a direct line-item return. Planning those landscapes to support biodiversity adds another dimension to that investment, allowing them to contribute to ecological health while serving the needs of the community.

Pollinators depend on more than a patch of flowers. They need plants that provide resources throughout the growing season, places to nest and landscapes they can move through. An isolated garden may offer some of those resources, but a coordinated network can support them across a larger area.

Research highlights how much landscape design can matter. A 2026 study published in Urban Ecosystems compared two newly developed residential neighborhoods and found that pollinator abundance and diversity were two to three times higher in the neighborhood dominated by native plants than in one with conventional landscaping. Despite similar numbers of flowers, the difference suggests that what developers plant can matter as much as how much they plant.

Master-planned communities have an unusual ability to create that network. Developers overseeing hundreds or thousands of acres can coordinate planting and habitat connections across property lines and development phases.

In a recent development, rather than treating pollinator-friendly landscaping as a one-time intervention, the strategy needs to evolve alongside the community. Establishing baseline ecological conditions before construction and continuing monitoring as development progresses creates a reference point to evaluate changes over time.

It has been revealed that that approach also requires considering habitat connectivity throughout the development process. Native plantings, open spaces and landscape corridors can be incorporated into the broader plan, rather than treated as isolated conservation features.

According to recent reports, as developers, we routinely track home sales, water use, construction costs and other indicators of a community’s performance. Tracking ecological outcomes brings that same discipline to landscape investments.

At Baseline, a 1,100-acre master-planned community in Broomfield, Colorado, Butterfly Pavilion introduced its Pollinator District model in 2019, integrating conservation into development and ongoing operations. With monitoring in place before construction, researchers recorded 3,805 macropollinators in developed areas in 2025, up from 587 in 2023, an increase of more than 500%.

Sources indicate that but numbers alone don’t tell the full story. Much of the increase came from nonnative western honeybees, making pollinator diversity an equally important measure of progress. The findings also highlight opportunities for additional native plantings to better support native bees.

It has been revealed that the broader lesson is that ecological performance can be measured, and those findings can inform future decisions. Pollinator counts alone cannot establish the impact of every landscape intervention, but monitoring provides a way to identify changes, evaluate habitat strategies and adjust as development progresses.

That same principle can apply beyond pollinators. Whether evaluating stormwater systems, native landscaping or habitat corridors, establishing meaningful measures of performance can help developers better understand the long-term outcomes of their investments.

Sources indicate that integrating biodiversity also creates an ongoing opportunity to learn. Working with ecological specialists helps developers understand the starting landscape, set meaningful goals and see how it responds. That work needs to carry into everyday landscape care, from what gets planted to how areas are mowed and pests are managed, with resources and responsibility for stewardship established for the years ahead.

According to recent reports, monitoring can guide future plant selections and help identify gaps in habitat connections as new neighborhoods take shape. It also requires consistency and an understanding that ecological conditions vary with weather, seasonal timing and other factors.

According to recent reports, protected lands and conservation areas remain essential to ecological health, but developed communities can contribute, too. Places designed for people can also provide meaningful habitat when ecological considerations are incorporated into planning and long-term operations.

According to recent reports, for developers, this is part of the longer commitment that comes with creating a master-planned community. These are places people will call home for decades, and caring for their ecological health is another part of planning for how they perform and evolve over that same horizon.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

In a recent development, why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026.

It has been revealed that AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

According to recent reports, they eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

According to recent reports, why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

Sources indicate that VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious initiative to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.
  • According to recent reports, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

According to recent reports, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid rapidly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Industry observers note that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

Sources indicate that “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he remarked. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

According to recent reports, “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd remarked. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in newly introduced natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

Industry observers note that he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

It has been revealed that redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he noted, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

Recent findings suggest that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion firm Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd mentioned he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

In a recent development, endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd noted there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The firm now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

It has been revealed that “This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise software giant SAP SE is reportedly planning to lay off at least 10,000 employees, or more than 9% of its workforce.
  • Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructuring initiative is still subject to change.
  • It has been revealed that according to the publication, SAP and a labor council in its home country of Germany have negotiated an “employment guarantee” that will run through 2028.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:20 EST / NOVEMBER 26 2026.

Enterprise software giant SAP SE is reportedly planning to lay off at least 10,000 employees, or more than 9% of its workforce.

Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the scope of the restructuring initiative is still subject to change.

It has been revealed that according to the publication, SAP and a labor council in its home country of Germany have negotiated an “employment guarantee” that will run through 2028. That may mean the layoffs will mainly affect employees in other markets. The report indicates that SAP’s product, engineering and sales units are expected to see the largest cuts.

Executives have reportedly also asked other departments to find cost reduction opportunities.

The reported restructuring push follows a banner quarter for SAP. The manufacturer’s sales and adjusted profit both topped analyst expectations. Its €24.11 billion cloud contract backlog, a measure of future revenue, also came in ahead of the consensus estimate.

Industry observers note that the planned layoffs are said to be connected to SAP’s efforts to integrate more artificial intelligence features into its products. The company is best known for its ERP, or enterprise resource planning, software. Enterprises use it to automate a long list of backoffice tasks and share data between teams. SAP also sells cloud services for other use cases such as sales automation and customer support.

Industry observers note that at a May user conference, the company introduced an AI interface called Joule Work for its applications. SAP says that the tool will enable workers to centrally access its products instead of navigating multiple screens.

Sources indicate that joule Work made its debut alongside a suite of AI agents dubbed Joule Assistants. According to SAP, they will use over 200 subagents to automate repetitive business tasks. Another newly introduced offering, Industry AI, will automate sector-specific workflows.

The report that SAP is preparing for job cuts doesn’t come as a complete surprise. Last week, Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam told attendees of an investor event that the firm expects its headcount to decline. Additionally, two of the software maker’s six directors will reportedly leave in connection with its shift to a more AI-centric strategy.

In a recent development, it’s unclear when the job cuts will take place. According to Bloomberg, SAP historically confirmed workforce reduction programs in January. The software maker took that route with its last major restructuring initiative, which saw it axe about 10,000 roles in 2024. The initiative cost about €3 billion.

The company remarked in a statement that “SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs.”.

#156513. Can Institutions Secretly Buy Billions of XRP? Ripple Veteran Indicates It Is 'Not Impossible'

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 U ↗ Open Full Page

Can Institutions Secretly Buy Billions of XRP? Ripple Veteran Indicates It Is 'Not Impossible'

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (412 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple’s longtime CTO emeritus David Schwartz does not think institutions can privately snap up billions of XRP via dark pools without affecting the token’s price on public markets.
  • Recent findings suggest that "I don't think so.
  • This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple’s longtime CTO emeritus David Schwartz does not think institutions can privately snap up billions of XRP via dark pools without affecting the token’s price on public markets.

Recent findings suggest that "I don't think so. Who are they buying the XRP from? Why wouldn't people generally want the price to rise when they buy? But it's not impossible," Schwartz wrote on X on Nov. 24.

This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.

Earlier in the conversation, Schwartz noted the pros and cons of dark pools for retail traders.

He mentioned one disadvantage: less efficient price discovery. Given that bids and offers are obscured, retail traders in public markets have less insight into other traders’ bids and ask prices.

If there is a large XRP holder who is already inclined to sell at the current price, an institution could arrange a private trade with this holder without needing to place a massive buy order on an exchange. They could execute the trade without driving the public price up as they buy.

In a recent development, however, will there be enough sellers interested in offloading billions of XRP like this? One might run out of sellers willing to sell at that price. So, the buyer might need to up the ante to find the next willing seller.

A dark pool can hide order size, but one still needs someone on the other side to execute that order.

Plus, a buyer will naturally prefer not to tip its hand while accumulating a position.

Schwartz left open the possibility of a private purchase at scale, but the possibility is rather low.

It has been revealed that when asked why XRP Ledger developments were not doing anything for XRP’s price on Nov. 9, Schwartz pointed to the broader crypto market.

Recent findings suggest that he also debunked the notion that Ripple had some secret plan it was not sharing with holders. The company regularly talks about its looks.

Schwartz also mentioned a practical benefit of XRP being worth more in the: a higher price could mean cheaper liquidity provision and less slippage (the difference between the expected price a trader pays and the price they actually pay).

At the same time, he was less convinced that demand for XRP to pay transaction fees could have a big impact on the price by itself.

NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO notes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Recent findings suggest that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents noted.

Recent findings suggest that pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO mentioned he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

According to recent reports, white also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”.

In a recent development, pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also stated the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

It has been revealed that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears stated the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

Sources indicate that “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” mentioned David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

In a recent development, pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Sources indicate that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a substantial decision to make in the next few weeks: take the firm’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Sources indicate that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a substantial decision to make in the next few weeks: take the firm’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Sources indicate that microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman revealed the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The tech giant expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

In a recent development, microsoft notes the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

Sources indicate that the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in newly introduced hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the organization decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a manufacturer right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

Industry observers note that there is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

According to recent reports, but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one firm.

Industry observers note that hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more crucial than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

According to recent reports, the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

Recent findings suggest that AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Sources indicate that software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

In a recent development, this cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

Recent findings suggest that the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

It has been revealed that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

1) Think VERY significant, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

Sources indicate that 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

In a recent development, there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Industry observers note that whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a new and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.
  • AI is identifying bugs in live software more quickly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.
  • As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a new and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.

AI is identifying bugs in live software more quickly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.

As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.

For Ethereum developers, the immediate challenge is ensuring that bugs are not present in their software before an upgrade.

In a recent development, the longer-term challenge is mathematical. Ethereum uses digital signatures to identify who can spend funds and which validators have approved the state of the chain.

Wedderburn indicates that AI's advances in analyzing decades-old algorithms raise questions about the mathematical assumptions underlying those signatures that researchers should consider.

According to recent reports, it is not clear whether AI could break Ethereum's existing cryptography. However,  the Ethereum Foundation wants work on new cryptography to be underway.

After more than a year of considering various signature schemes, the Ethereum Foundation has decided to replace elliptic-curve signatures with hash-based cryptography.

The argument is that Ethereum already relies on cryptographic hash security, and by using hashes for signatures too, it can remove an additional assumption about the difficulty of solving mathematical problems associated with elliptic curves.

The proposal affects three areas of Ethereum.

It would see validators use hash-based keys for their signatures, which in turn changes how block finality is determined on the network.

Wallet developers would need to provide users with a way to transition their accounts to hash-based signatures.

And Ethereum's change to the cryptography used for commitments to data (blobs) that rollups publish to the network would require adjustments from rollups too.

Industry observers note that one challenge is the size of the signatures. Hash-based signatures are much larger, so developers need to consider how that affects the hardware needed to run a node at home.

Sources indicate that staking pools and multisig wallets would need adjustments too. So would smart contracts that rely on existing cryptography.

There will also be a need to adjust tools that rely on the signature scheme currently used by Ethereum validators (BLS).

In a recent development, WILLIAMSVILLE, N.Y., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What happens at your first ballroom lesson? The article explains that many first-time students arrive with questions about what they will be asked to do and whether previous experience is required. According to the feature, beginner ballroom dancing is designed with upcoming dancers in mind, allowing students to learn at a comfortable pace without feeling pressured to keep up with anyone else.

According to recent reports, the feature also emphasizes that no prior dance experience is necessary. Many students arrive for their first ballroom lesson without knowing any dance steps, and instructors expect beginners to start from the basics. According to the article, lessons are structured to introduce simple movements one at a time, helping students develop confidence as each latest skill builds naturally on the last.

Industry observers note that the article explains that early instruction often focuses on fundamental skills such as footwork, rhythm, posture, balance, and partner connection. These concepts provide the foundation for future ballroom dance lessons while remaining approachable for upcoming students. By introducing these basics gradually, instructors help students feel successful from the very beginning.

Readers also learn that students can participate whether they arrive with a partner or attend alone. The article explains that many dance studios provide instructors or practice partners when needed, allowing anyone interested in beginner ballroom dancing to participate comfortably. This flexibility helps make ballroom dancing accessible to a wide range of students.

Recent findings suggest that another point highlighted in the article is that making mistakes is an expected part of learning. The dance instructor encourages questions, provides corrections, and allows students time to practice without feeling rushed. Rather than viewing mistakes as setbacks, the article describes them as valuable opportunities that help students improve with each lesson.

In a recent development, the feature also discusses the pace of instruction during a first ballroom lesson. Instead of introducing numerous dances at once, instructors typically focus on mastering a few basic movements correctly before moving forward. This steady approach helps students retain what they have learned while building confidence through consistent progress.

Recent findings suggest that the article also offers practical guidance about preparing for the lesson itself. Comfortable clothing that allows easy movement and secure shoes are generally all that is needed for a first visit to a dance studio. Special dance attire is rarely necessary, allowing beginners to focus on learning rather than worrying about what to wear.

Recent findings suggest that as the lesson concludes, many students discover they have learned more than they expected in a single session. The article notes that initial nervousness often gives way to confidence as basic movements become more familiar. Regular ballroom dance lessons continue to build on that foundation, helping students develop upcoming skills while enjoying the movement, social connection, and satisfaction that come with steady improvement.

Industry News: Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.
  • The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors.
  • The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

Industry observers note that in a blog post, Amazon noted it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the manufacturer wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Latest York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

Amazon introduced its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a recent development, in a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel mentioned the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the organization works with in the city and the more than 5,000 Fresh Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel noted. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The tech giant also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its intends for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most Latest Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Latest Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

It has been revealed that city leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” remarked Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Newly introduced Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The firm said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in Upcoming York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Jensen Huang’s back, and not everyone is happy with that.

Nvidia’s board reversed the resignation of its former and current-again CEO Monday, apparently under pressure from the well-known business genius and lame-duck President Donald Trump, who worried that the stock market and the AI trade would suffer without him at the helm.

Huang (pictured) clearly has management talent, having built one of the most valuable companies in the world. But his return, amid continuing revelations and questions about Nvidia’s business, sets an awful precedent in business. No one person should be too important to fail, and Huang set up a corporate structure that courts disaster if he’s forced to leave again or gets run over by a bus. That’s a world-class failure of a CEO and his board at one of their most basic jobs, and his tech-bro enablers should know better than to clamor for his return.

After all, internal and government investigations continue, as more details come to light about probably the worst of the whole affair(s). It’s clear that at a time when there’s existential worry about China closing the U.S. lead in AI — a potential defense and cybersecurity disaster — the chief supplier of AI chips was allowing cutting-edge chips to be sent to China. Oh, and this week’s stock market pretty much discounted much of the supposed benefit Huang’s reinstatement was supposed to provide.

Recent findings suggest that so what are we left with? The CEO of the pivotal manufacturer in AI is back with not even a slap on the wrist, let alone any consequences for multiple affairs — one with a woman who shuttled both barred GPUs and apparently inside information to China, another with an Nvidia VP, plus at least a couple others he fessed up to. Oh, and he lied about them until he couldn’t anymore. Any semblance of corporate governance and ethics — at Nvidia and everywhere else by example — is utterly torched.

According to recent reports, hey, if you think that’s a buying opportunity, I’ve got some high-end GPUs in Singapore to sell you. Anyway, let’s move on before I tell you what I really think.

Last week Palo Alto Networks stated it will acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. This week was CrowdStrike’s turn, as it pulled the trigger on buying Zscaler for a pretty stunning $44 billion. As AI makes cyberattacks far easier and more numerous, it seems a sure bet that today’s rickety cybersecurity industry with hundred of point products won’t stand.
