#156502. The referral source real estate agents overlook is sitting in the next office

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

The referral source real estate agents overlook is sitting in the next office

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve spent more than 25 years in this business, and one pattern has held strong in every market I’ve worked in: the agents who build lasting careers rarely do it alone.
  • According to recent reports, referrals between agents get less attention than they deserve.
  • In a recent development, your brokerage is the most natural place to begin, and it’s often the most overlooked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve spent more than 25 years in this business, and one pattern has held strong in every market I’ve worked in: the agents who build lasting careers rarely do it alone. They have a network of fellow agents who think of them first when a client needs help. At The Agency, we were built on that idea. We encourage our agents to reach across the aisle, even to competitors, because when agents collaborate, more deals get done and clients are better served.

According to recent reports, referrals between agents get less attention than they deserve. We talk constantly about our sphere of influence, past clients and social media. Yet a colleague who’s relocating a client to your market, or who’s overbooked and can’t take on a upcoming listing, might hand you a deal worth far more than a month of lead generation. Those opportunities only come to agents who’ve earned a place in someone’s mind.

In a recent development, your brokerage is the most natural place to begin, and it’s often the most overlooked. Most of us share an office, a leadership team and a set of tools with dozens or even hundreds of agents, and many of us barely know their names.

According to recent reports, introduce yourself. Show up at the sales meeting, the training and the broker open, and stay for the conversation afterward. Ask people what they specialize in, what kind of client they love working with, and what they’d happily hand off. You’ll learn who’s the go-to for condos, who knows the hillside neighborhoods best, and who’s the strongest negotiator in the building.

Sources indicate that that knowledge pays off rapidly. When a client mentions a need outside your expertise, you’ll know exactly who to call. When a colleague gets a request that fits your strengths, they’ll know to call you. Trust inside a brokerage builds slowly, but once it’s there, it makes everyone’s business stronger.

Recent findings suggest that competition is part of this industry, and I won’t pretend otherwise. But the agent across the street at another firm is also a potential partner, and the best ones treat them that way.

Think about how much of real estate is geographic. Clients move across the country, across the state, sometimes across town into a different market. Your client in Los Angeles who’s buying in Aspen needs someone they can trust on the ground, and you can’t be that person. A thoughtful agent in Aspen, whom you’ve met and vetted, can. The same goes in reverse. That’s a referral built on mutual respect, and it often leads to repeat business flowing both ways for years.

It has been revealed that industry events, local board committees and MLS involvement are all excellent places to meet these people. You see how people handle disagreement, how they treat staff, and how they follow through. That’s the kind of insight no online profile will give you.

If you want referrals, you have to be worth referring. When one agent sends a client to another, they’re putting their own reputation on the line. They want to know that their client will be taken care of, that communication will be prompt, and that the deal will be handled with integrity.

So treat every interaction with another agent as an audition, whether or not it’s a referral situation. Return calls promptly. Show up prepared. Be the person who makes a tough negotiation easier instead of harder. Agents remember who was gracious under pressure, and they remember who wasn’t.

It has been revealed that close the loop, too. If someone sends you a client, keep them updated and thank them, even when the deal takes months. It sounds small, but plenty of agents forget, and the ones who don’t stand out.

I’d encourage agents to build  a simple structure around this. Set a goal to connect with a few new agents each month, one or two inside your brokerage and a few outside it. Grab coffee or hop on a quick call. Send a note when you see a colleague’s listing go under contract. Ask how you can be useful before you ask for anything.

It doesn’t take much time, just consistency and a willingness to see other agents as allies. Your next client might be working with an agent down the hall right now, or with one in a brokerage across the country. Sooner or later, that client will ask for a recommendation. Make sure the agent who gets asked already knows you.

Rainy Hake Austin is a brokerage leader at The Agency.

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has confirmed a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the manufacturer’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

According to recent reports, in August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly unveiled investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, stated today in a news release.

Sources indicate that “By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith mentioned. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the firm’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas mentioned.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) community members have launched a latest block explorer for Shibarium, the layer-2 network of the SHIB ecosystem, and Shiba Inu lead Shytoshi Kusama has remained silent on X since May.

In a recent development, shiba Inu community veteran Mazrael confirmed the new explorer, scan.shibfun.app, in an X post. "Shibarium has a new block explorer," he wrote. According to Mazrael, the explorer was "built by the community, powered by ShibWatch, dressed in the Eternity Hub look.".

The launch comes as SHIB trades near its lowest levels in years. In November, the price of SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021, and on Nov. 22, the token traded at around $0.00000362, according to CoinMarketCap.

It has been revealed that according to the post, people can type a .shib name in the search bar and land on the wallet linked to it, and the explorer also indicates new Shiboshis from Shibarium every day. For developers, Mazrael listed contract verification, read and write functions for contracts, the activity of ERC-4337 smart wallets, and a free API, which he described as "Etherscan-style too." Method names are decoded as well, and in Mazrael's words, there are "no more mystery 0x codes." The explorer also has a DApps page with Shibarium games and apps, and a button that adds Shibarium to a wallet in one click.

Sources indicate that the work on the explorer is not finished yet. "Live blocks are complete now, and older history indexing," Mazrael wrote. On Tuesday, the explorer itself demonstrated that 3% of Shibarium blocks had been indexed, and a notice on the site noted that some of the counts may be inaccurate. Mazrael added that the latest explorer can be found on Shib.io under ShibWatch.

Shytoshi Kusama's last post or interaction on X dates back to May 13, 2026. In September, Kusama changed his X bio to "Polish" and his location to "Close," and he has not explained the meaning of either word. The official Shibarium account on X has not posted since July 13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that still, Shibarium updates kept coming from community members. In October, Mazrael mentioned that CreateX, a standard factory for deploying contracts at the same address on different chains, went live on Shibarium. According to Mazrael, all 12 Safe v1.4.1 contracts were deployed to their canonical addresses through the Safe Singleton Factory, and x402 went live too, so AI agents can now pay in SHIB, TREAT and wrapped BONE.

In September 2025, attackers exploited the Shibarium bridge and withdrew about $2.4 million worth of assets from it.

Sources indicate that according to Shibariumscan, Shibarium processed 546 transactions in a single day in late November, and on Oct. 31, the daily number of transactions on the network was 6,370. Since its launch in August 2023, Shibarium has processed more than 1.5 billion transactions in total.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan.

  • 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Do you need a trust or is a will enough?
  • Industry observers note that the article explains that many people begin estate planning by asking whether they need a trust or a will.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jennifer McKenna explains how trusts and wills work together to support an estate planning strategy based on individual needs.

LEE'S SUMMIT, Mo., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Do you need a trust or is a will enough? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Estate Planning Attorney Jennifer McKenna of the Jennifer Ward McKenna, Attorney at Law in Lees Summit, Missouri, explains how trusts and wills serve different purposes within an estate planning strategy.

Industry observers note that the article explains that many people begin estate planning by asking whether they need a trust or a will. The answer depends on factors such as family circumstances, financial goals, the types of assets they own, and how they want those assets managed after death. The article notes that both legal tools play important roles and understanding their differences helps individuals make informed decisions.

Recent findings suggest that according to the article, a will is a legal document that explains how a person's property should be distributed after death. It also allows someone to name an executor to manage the estate and nominate guardians for minor children when necessary. The article describes a will as the foundation of many estate planning prepares because it provides clear instructions and guidance for loved ones during a difficult time.

In a recent development, the HelloNation article also explains that a will always goes through the probate process after death. During probate, the court validates the will, oversees the payment of debts, and authorizes the distribution of assets. While probate is a routine legal process, the article notes that the timeline depends on the amount of assets administered through the will, the complexity of the estate, and state law. Some estates move through probate relatively promptly, while most require several months to resolve legal or administrative matters.

Industry observers note that A trust serves a different purpose by allowing assets to be managed by a trustee for the benefit of designated beneficiaries. Unlike a will, many assets held in a properly funded trust can pass directly to beneficiaries without going through probate. The article explains that avoiding probate is one of the primary reasons some individuals include a trust as part of an overall estate planning strategy. It also notes that a trust can provide instructions for managing assets if the person creating the trust becomes unable to manage financial matters during their lifetime or when a beneficiary is unable to manage an inheritance effectively, such as a young child or an individual with special needs.

Recent findings suggest that the article emphasizes that a trust is not automatically the right choice for every family. Establishing and maintaining a trust requires additional planning, and assets must be properly transferred into the trust for it to function as intended. If assets remain outside the trust, they may still be subject to probate. The article explains that understanding how a trust works is just as crucial as deciding whether to create one.

Rather than viewing these documents as alternatives, the article explains that a will and a trust often work together. A trust may be used to manage significant assets, while a will can address property that was not transferred into the trust and nominate guardians for minor children. According to the article, this combination creates a more complete estate planning approach that reflects a family's specific circumstances and long-term goals.

The article also notes that every estate is different, and no single solution works for everyone. Some individuals focus on protecting young children, while others are more concerned with managing business interests, real estate, or investment accounts. Estate planning allows legal documents to reflect those priorities instead of relying on general assumptions.

Sources indicate that the article concludes that delaying estate planning because of uncertainty about choosing a trust or a will can leave notable questions unanswered. Learning how a trust, a will, and probate work allows individuals to make informed decisions that fit their own circumstances. Whether someone ultimately chooses a will, a trust, or both, taking time to understand these legal tools can provide greater clarity and help protect loved ones in the future.

Do You Need a Trust or Is a Will Enough? Features insights from Jennifer McKenna, Estate Planning Attorney of Lees Summit, Missouri, in HelloNation.

#156497. Latest Update: Who should referee a national MLS, brokers or a neutral body?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1163 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Who should referee a national MLS, brokers or a neutral body?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Open Real Estate was confirmed, the question of a national listing system moved back to the center of our industry.
  • Industry observers note that first, credit where it is due.
  • I see two problems, one practical and one structural, and the structural one is the one that should concern every leader who does not run one of the three or four largest firms in the country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Open Real Estate was confirmed, the question of a national listing system moved back to the center of our industry. I am early in my read on this particular initiative. But I have spent a long time on the underlying question, enough that I have written a white paper of more than 70 pages on why a broker-controlled national MLS is the wrong design and what a right one would look like. For the leaders reading this, I want to lay out the core of that thinking, because this is a decision our industry may actually make in the next few years, and we should make it with our eyes open.

Industry observers note that first, credit where it is due. A coalition of large brokerages banded together and put their names to a public position. That takes coordination and conviction, and it is plainly a response to a real and growing trend, the migration of listings into private and exclusive channels that never touch the open market. The concern is legitimate. When inventory moves into walled gardens, buyers see less, agents compete on access instead of expertise, and the consumer is quietly disadvantaged. Leaders who are worried about that are worried about the right thing.

I see two problems, one practical and one structural, and the structural one is the one that should concern every leader who does not run one of the three or four largest firms in the country.

The practical problem is straightforward. The founders have stated that Open Real Estate is not a national MLS and is not meant to replace local MLSs. Whatever we call it, it is built to function as shared national listing infrastructure, and that infrastructure includes a participant view option, where a listing can be seen only by agents at participating brokerages and cannot be publicly marketed by anyone. In other words, the model does not stop private listings. It gives them a larger, better-organized home. The exact behavior this is meant to counter can continue, and we have built a bigger shared system that still has walls inside it.

According to recent reports, consider the architecture we have now. Hundreds of local MLSs operate across the country. We complain about that fragmentation endlessly, and it does create real friction for agents and consumers. But the fragmentation also delivers a benefit almost no one names. Each MLS acts as its own silo, its own firewall. Because the data lives in hundreds of independent repositories, no single manufacturer controls the national market. There is a series called Silo that captures the idea well. Each silo runs itself, and no one can command the whole system. Our MLS structure has handed us that same protection almost by accident. The walls are inconvenient, and the walls are also the reason no one firm owns the country’s data.

Now collapse all of it into one national system, whatever label it carries, and ask the only question that matters. Who runs it? If the answer is that brokers run it, then the brokers with the deepest pockets will control the nation’s listing infrastructure. The independents, the single-office shops, the regional firms, they will have little to no voice. Whoever sits atop a broker-controlled national system writes the rules for everyone downstream, including their direct competitors. That is not a free market with shared plumbing. That is a tollgate owned by a few, and everyone else pays to pass through.

Recent findings suggest that powerfact: Whoever controls a national MLS controls the terms of competition for every agent in the country. That cannot be a competitor.

So, let me be clear that I am not against unification. A national MLS done correctly would be a real asset. It would let an agent see listings nationwide rather than stitching together access market by market. It would mean one playbook, the same rules, forms, and fields in every state, so practicing across state lines or relocating would not require relearning the mechanics each time. That consistency would benefitagents, brokers, and consumers. The debate should not be unify or do not unify. The fight is already here, and it should be about who holds the technology in the middle.

In a recent development, and we already have a proven answer inside our own economy. Visa and MasterCard.

According to recent reports, the first bank card came from Bank of America. When other banks saw it working, each began building its own card and its own processing, and the result was chaos, because every bank set different rules and the consumer experience depended on which card you carried. The resolution was not to let the largest bank operate everyone else’s cards. It was Visa, a separate entity sitting in the middle. Each bank still runs its own business and competes on its own terms. The technology and the standards that make the system uniform for the consumer are handled by a neutral party that no single bank owns.

That is the template for a national MLS. Not control by the largest brokerages, but a neutral, broker-independent organization that operates the technology and maintains uniform rules, while every brokerage, large and small, continues to run its own business and compete on skill and service. Keep each firm a silo where it should be a silo. Make the shared rails in the middle belong to no one in particular. That is the only structure that stays fair to the smallest independent and the largest franchise at the same time.

When the next national platform is announced, and there will be more of them, do not evaluate it on the feature list. Evaluate it on governance. Ask who owns it, who sits on the board, how the rules get changed, and what recourse a small brokerage has if the controlling firms decide to change the terms. If the governance concentrates power in a handful of competitors, the convenience on the surface is not worth the dependency underneath. If the governance looks like Visa, neutral, independent, and accountable to all participants rather than to the biggest ones, then we may finally have something worth building.

I appreciate the effort behind Open Real Estate, and I share the concern that prompted it. But good intentions do not fix bad architecture. A national listing system run by brokers would trade the problem of private listings for the larger problem of a privatized commons, owned by the few and rented to the many. We can do better, and we have a model sitting in our wallets that demonstrates us how. Build the referee first. Then build the league.

In a recent development, darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

Recent findings suggest that orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

According to recent reports, “Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu noted in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

Sources indicate that the startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

It has been revealed that possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any prepares to move the testnet launch to another day.

Industry observers note that flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

Sources indicate that why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

Industry observers note that that’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has mentioned the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 owners may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity notes it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

Recent findings suggest that how it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

Sources indicate that more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the manufacturer claims, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a tech giant’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-newly introduced releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity notes its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

According to recent reports, the tech giant has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

According to recent reports, what’s next: StepSecurity intends to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The tech giant indicates it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency users following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.".

Industry observers note that according to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

According to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that the device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

The user said $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

According to recent reports, another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim says they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

On November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is currently no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

In a recent development, trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are currently no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

@OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official ENHANCEMENT: This device came directly from Trezor and shows no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

In a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the manufacturer and demonstrated no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

Industry observers note that this appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an vital security warning: consumers should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

#156490. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1901 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • In a recent development, now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

In a recent development, now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous upgrade that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

It has been revealed that the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella noted Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella stated, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

Sources indicate that MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

Industry observers note that MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a tech giant partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

It has been revealed that since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

In a recent development, what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the organization with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Recent findings suggest that most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from fresh finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

In a recent development, moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

In a recent development, no surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

In a recent development, microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple customers to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

According to recent reports, the cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to glitch OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

According to recent reports, OOBs are key enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Industry observers note that think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Sources indicate that here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Sources indicate that even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It has been revealed that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

Recent findings suggest that what needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

In periods of competing blocks, Solana validators spend CPU and timing resources replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another competing block from the same slot has been finalized.

Recent findings suggest that this PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done. It also decouples functionality and gives control to Votor in requesting slot cancellation without modifying BankForks.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this is a reasonable technical improvement and has a good engineering motivation. Further technical comments and review would be helpful to understand if there are potential race conditions or concerns with reliability of replay and consensus. This could be split into two PRs to make it easier to test and review.

There are two main proposed changes:.

Make sure that the replay thread doesn't block on the scheduler finishing processing blocks.

Add slot cancellation, where Votor can tell replay which blocks to stop trying to process.

There was an earlier PR (PR #16454) which attempted to solve a similar problem, but that PR included some complexity around being able to pause and resume block processing.

In a recent development, this PR attempts to solve a similar problem in a simpler way by adding slot cancellation. It allows validators to stop replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another block from the same slot has been finalized.

It has been revealed that this is an efficiency-focused change to validator software. It's not intended to have a particular effect on transaction throughput or SOL price. For Solana to continue to perform well, it's key not only to continue to increase TPS but also continue to find ways to make sure that validators aren't doing unnecessary work.

For everyday people, it's unlikely there would be noticeable effects from this change. Sending/receiving SOL, using a DEX, using DeFi more broadly, and using any other Solana-powered website/app should all continue to function as normal. It's possible that users could see some benefits from this change in the form of Solana being more performant in the face of heavy compute loads.

Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless.
  • Sources indicate that few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa.
  • She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months.

Sources indicate that few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to.

She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.

But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility.

In a recent development, U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy, younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars.

A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same significant names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers.

“You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural credibility or this idea of being cool,” Izzy Farmiloe, global head of strategy and growth at Dazed Studio, the agency arm of youth culture and fashion publisher Dazed Media, told Fortune.

Long before Instagram gave celebrities a place to document their breakfast, much of the fascination with the cool girl came from how little the public knew about her.

Recent findings suggest that in a November essay for his newsletter, Considered Chaos, brand strategist Eugene Healey explained how each generation’s cool girl was shaped by the media of her time. Kate Moss had fashion magazines, the Olsen twins had the paparazzi, and Alexa Chung had fashion blogs and street-style photographers.

Social media brought audiences closer to the women they admired, making relatability an asset for personalities like Emma Chamberlain. As algorithms began serving up content based on people’s interests rather than simply who they followed, celebrities also had more reason to venture beyond the industries that made them famous.

“Dua Lipa was made for the feed,” Healey wrote.

Her friendship with designer Simon Porte Jacquemus might draw in fashion enthusiasts, while her book club could introduce her to someone who has never listened to Future Nostalgia. Each new audience offers another opportunity to make money beyond selling records and concert tickets.

Sources indicate that it’s a business model that has become increasingly familiar, with celebrities launching beauty brands, starting newsletters, and inviting followers into their kitchens. Somewhere along the way, having a favorite lip gloss became an opportunity to launch a cosmetics company.

Recent findings suggest that the trouble with making a living off being cool is that the more people see someone being paid to recommend things, the harder it becomes to tell what she actually likes. Even the seemingly casual Instagram photo dump, filled with blurry pictures and half-eaten meals, can be as carefully curated as the polished posts it was meant to replace.

For Jenna Drenten, a marketing professor at Loyola University Chicago, the problem lies in the very nature of an influencer’s job. “They are expected to sell what is popular, but also expected to discover what’s new,” Drenten told Fortune.

Sources indicate that drenten pointed to BookTok, where recommending a novel outside the usual bestseller rotation can set a creator apart. If enough people take her advice, however, the book becomes just another BookTok sensation, losing some of the very appeal that made it worth recommending in the first place.

Sources indicate that brands risk falling into the same trap. Farmiloe has seen companies chase the same trends and hire the same talent in their pursuit of relevance, spending money only to end up looking more like one another.

“I actually think silence can often be a stronger strategy now,” Farmiloe said.

It has been revealed that trying too hard to look polished may also backfire for brands, especially as artificial intelligence makes it easier to produce everything from flawless images to cultural recommendations. “To sort of show mistakes is a way of proving that a human has made something,” Farmiloe said, adding that even typos have become chic.

Healey identified three potential successors to the Dua Lipa era: the obsessive, who knows a particular subject inside and out; the ghost, whose reputation spreads without constantly posting; and the host, who brings people together in real life.

He argued that the three share expertise and charisma that are hard to fake at a moment when faking has never been easier. If the next dominant medium is an AI model that can summarize the world’s knowledge on demand, Healey wrote, cool becomes whatever can’t be summarized.

For brands accustomed to measuring influence in followers, likes, and views, the next cool girl may be much harder to price. Drenten sees growing appeal in people who can offer something beyond a product recommendation, whether it’s a longtime librarian who can introduce readers to literature they might never have discovered on their own or someone who brings strangers together outside the confines of their carefully curated feeds.

It has been revealed that as going out becomes increasingly expensive, Farmiloe sees an opportunity for brands to help create those experiences. She pointed to Reference Point, a London library, bookshop, and bar that doubles as a gathering place for chess, poetry, and jazz.

Rather than paying someone to talk about a brand, companies could give people a place to spend time together.

“Instead of just getting noticed, how do you get people to care or actually like engage or spend time with your brand?” Farmiloe mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Recent findings suggest that A latest baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

Recent findings suggest that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla mentioned. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

In a recent development, to spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has challenges with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and Newly introduced Jersey.

Gangiredla stated the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

It has been revealed that if you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla remarked. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

According to recent reports, the platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for consumers.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

According to recent reports, birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

Sources indicate that how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — substantial metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your firm?

According to recent reports, it’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Sources indicate that earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our company has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms.“It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social.

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”.

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

Recent findings suggest that on Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”.

Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan remarked in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).”.

“Data revisions are more common as structural change and poor survey response rates reduce precision.”.

In a recent development, but President Trump suggested there were more nefarious reasons for the near-percentage-point difference in initial estimates to the published figures: “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.”.

Recent findings suggest that lutnick issued a bullish economic enhancement. Writing on X, the Commerce Secretary said: “We’re bringing American manufacturing back at a scale nobody thought possible. America’s successes will become even more powerful in the coming years as these projects move from groundbreaking to full production.”.

Sources indicate that trump’s latest clash with federal data agencies could further undermine confidence in U.S. economic statistics. In 2025, the president fired the director of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Erika McEntarfer, claiming she had overseen the publishing of “phony” job numbers for political reasons. (The president provided no evidence for his claim.).

Recent findings suggest that this, paired with Trump’s extraordinary attacks on the Federal Reserve under former chairman Jerome Powell, led many economists and investors to worry about the credibility of major U.S. institutions that either inform policy or make it.

At the time, Alberto Cavallo, Professor at Harvard Business School, told Goldman Sachs: “It’s difficult to avoid a comparison to the experience of my home country, Argentina, nearly two decades ago when the president, dismayed at rising inflation, removed statistical agency leadership.

According to recent reports, “Some statistics stopped being reported, and official data no longer seemed to align with perceptions. That was a very chaotic period that destroyed trust in Argentina’s official statistics for over a decade.”.

Retailers offering freebies and rebates this holiday weekend expect something in return: a trip to the store and more spending once the shopper is inside. In an ICSC survey reported by TheStreet, 49% of shoppers say they're worried about affording holiday gifts, and 68% say discounts and promotions will get them shopping in stores more. A holiday reward aimed at these shoppers is a bargain with two sides, and the retailer has already set the terms.

Kohl's $KSS is offering its own reward over the holiday weekend while fewer people come into its stores. Its store visits are down 1.4%, according to Placer.ai figures, so any offer that brings shoppers back has clear value. Its standard reward, Kohl's Cash, arrives only after a purchase as store currency, and the rules attached to it decide how much of the printed amount a shopper actually keeps.

Kohl's lays out its Kohl's Cash rules and the giveaways it ran over the Nov. 27–29 holiday weekend, from how the qualifying spend is counted to what a return does to rewards already issued. Shoppers who plan their purchases around these rules keep more of the reward than shoppers who don't.

Industry observers note that kohl's $KSS Cash rewards a shopper according to the size of one purchase: $15 back for each $50 spent in a single transaction during the Black Friday event. The reward rises only in $50 steps, so a basket that stops short of the next step earns nothing for the extra items in it. That gives shoppers a reason to add one more item to reach the next step.

Kohl's paid $10 for every $50 during its Deal Days, Oct. 6–8, 2026, so the rate changes from event to event. Shoppers should check the current rate before planning a purchase around it.

Kohl's sets the promotion's hours in Central Time, so a shopper in a western time zone who waits until the last evening by their own clock may find the offer has already ended.

The rate pays off best for shoppers who were going to spend that much at Kohl's.

Recent findings suggest that the spending that counts toward Kohl's $KSS Cash is the total after markdowns and coupons, with tax and shipping left out. Every coupon a shopper uses also lowers the amount Kohl's counts, so anyone aiming for the threshold should add up the merchandise after discounts before reaching the register.

Kohl's also counts each purchase on its own, so two smaller orders placed over the weekend don't add together toward the threshold. A shopper who usually spreads gift buying across several trips can reach the threshold more easily by pulling those purchases into one larger order.

Industry observers note that kohl's $KSS, not the shopper, decides the order of discounts at checkout, and the dollar-off value of Kohl's Cash comes off before any percent-off coupon. The coupon's percentage then applies to the smaller total, so a shopper who stacks a coupon on top of Kohl's Cash should expect the combined savings to come in a little lower than the two added together.

Sources indicate that spending Kohl's Cash doesn't require a second trip to the store. Kohl's accepts the reward on its website as well as at its stores and kiosks, and each of those options still ends in a.

A Kohl's $KSS Cash voucher stays tied to the purchase that earned it. A shopper who brings an item back may get a smaller refund than expected, and Kohl's may also adjust Kohl's Cash it has already issued.

Recent findings suggest that the rule covers items bought with Kohl's Cash as well as items that earned it, and Kohl's gives no formula for how much a return takes back. Anyone unsure about a gift, a size or a color should treat the Kohl's Cash it earned as provisional until they're sure they'll keep the item.

It has been revealed that A shopper doesn't use Kohl's $KSS Cash to lower the bill for the purchase that earns it. Kohl's complications the reward after the sale as a separate voucher, by email, printed on the receipt or inside the Kohl's app, and each of those is something the shopper has to keep track of until the next trip.

The sensible habit is to ask at the register how the reward was sent, then save that email, tuck the receipt somewhere safe or check the app before leaving the parking lot.

A shopper collects the rebate only by still holding it when it's time to spend.

A shopper can lose some vouchers entirely. Kohl's applies forfeiture to promotional vouchers under the terms of each offer, not to all Kohl's Cash, so a shopper should read the terms of any voucher that came from a promotion.

Kohl's Cash can be spent anywhere Kohl's sells, but promotional vouchers come with their own fine print.

Sources indicate that gift cards, taxes, shipping and fees are excluded from both earning and redeeming Kohl's $KSS Cash. Gift cards matter most to holiday buyers: a gift card purchase earns nothing toward the reward, and a shopper can't convert Kohl's Cash into a gift card.

Even when Kohl's Cash covers every item in the bag, the shopper still pays these costs in real money.

Keep the item before you spend the reward it earned.

It has been revealed that each Kohl's $KSS store handed its first 200 customers on Friday a voucher worth between $5 and $100, no purchase required. Those vouchers are Kohl's Cash, according to NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth, so even the free prize can be spent only at Kohl's.

Stores opened at 5 a.m. on Friday, Nov. 27, and only shoppers near the front of the line got a voucher. Kohl's followed on Saturday, Nov. 28, with a second giveaway of Sephora coupons.

Sources indicate that kohl's spreads its giveaway across many shoppers but keeps the top prize modest. At Academy Sports + Outdoors, only 100 shoppers per store get a voucher, but those run from $20 up to $500. The one Kohl's giveaway paid in money a shopper can spend anywhere is the $10,000 cash sweepstakes, and entering offers only a chance at it.

What Kohl's gives away for free this weekend is mostly built to come back to Kohl's.

The extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

As the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

This is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

Those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

It has been revealed that the acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

Sources indicate that for the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration challenges before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

Support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

The technical issue was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

That’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.

  • According to recent reports, microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their newly introduced home.
  • Microsoft prepares to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm.

According to recent reports, microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their newly introduced home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Microsoft prepares to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the organization’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft notes Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

In a recent development, why Microsoft is doing it: The firm said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A newly introduced Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Owners weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft confirmed Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

According to recent reports, rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

In a recent development, the most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and stated it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

According to recent reports, reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent organization, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist consumers may end up back with the people who built it.
