💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow.
  • According to recent reports, around 44% of employers strategy to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report.
  • Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

According to recent reports, around 44% of employers strategy to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the latest compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

According to recent reports, “Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a big concern.”.

Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

In a recent development, while U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses plan to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks confirmed it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader company turnaround effort.

It has been revealed that but Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke mentioned, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”.

As more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

Industry observers note that U.S. CEO John Furner said it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually.

And with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 2, 2026.

Tech Report: 10 last-minute Black Friday tricks to check before you pay today

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A selection of 10 Black Friday tricks for shoppers heading out today, and how to check each one against the price before you pay.
  • If you're shopping today, the sale price doesn't have to be the final price.
  • In a recent development, that checking matters, because the extras don't always stack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A selection of 10 Black Friday tricks for shoppers heading out today, and how to check each one against the price before you pay.

If you're shopping today, the sale price doesn't have to be the final price. You can sometimes shave off more with a card that earns rewards, cash back after the fact, a promo code or a free gift. Black Friday falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, so there's no weekend left to initiative. Whatever checking you do will happen in the aisle or on your phone.

In a recent development, that checking matters, because the extras don't always stack. Rakuten's own help center warns that using a coupon code the site doesn't list can void your cash back. It also notes that some stores won't pay cash back on any part of a purchase covered by a gift card. Pile on every trick at once and you can end up worse off than someone who picked one carefully. The real skill today is knowing which extra to use on which purchase, not grabbing all of them.

The headline offer rarely tells the whole story, either. Some retailers don't bother waiting for Friday. Target's Black Friday sale started Sunday, Nov. 22, so a "Black Friday deal" you see there today may have been sitting there for days. The flashiest perks often come with strings. Target's in-store gift card giveaway went only to the first 100 people in line at each store, who received cards worth $25, $50 or $100. One person per store got a $1,000 card, and tickets had to be redeemed within an hour of the 6 a.m. opening. Discounted gift cards are everywhere this week too. KCRA reports offers like up to 25% off at Sam's Club and up to 20% off select cards at Best Buy. But a discounted gift card only saves you money if it's for a store you'll actually shop at.

Industry observers note that NBC News Select's Black Friday guide lays out the main ways to cut costs. They include discounted gift cards, cash-back portals and apps, rewards credit cards, gifts with purchase, price-history trackers and price-adjustment policies. Some of these quietly hand back money on things you were going to buy anyway. Others work better as warnings about how retailers dress up a price. Either way, each one only pays off on top of a price you've already checked. That's the test every tactic here has to pass.

A discounted gift card doesn't lower the price of any one product. It lowers the cost of the money you pay with, so the saving lands on top of whatever markdown is already on the shelf. Pay $90 for a $100 card and you've knocked another $10 off, while still getting the store's own sale price. The catch is that the card only works at a store that takes it. That means you pick the store first and the card second. A cheap card for a store you weren't planning to visit just ties up your money. If you're still shopping this weekend, buy a card only for a store that's already on your list, not a stack of cheap cards on the off chance you'll use them.

In a recent development, how much you save depends on which card you buy and where you buy it. On Black Friday, Bass Pro Shops and Cabela's were taking 10% off holiday gift cards, and inKind cards were 30% off on Amazon, KCRA reported. The Amazon offers were Lightning Deals that end once they sell out, so check before counting on them. Shop for the card the way you'd shop for the item it's paying for, because the first discount you see may not be the deepest. Warehouse clubs are a good place to look. Sam's Club advertised up to 25% off gift cards, and BJ's had 18% off a Barnes & Noble card. Costco's gift-card discounts are for members only, though. If you don't belong, judge the deal you can actually get, not the best one you've read about.

Some "gift card deals" don't make the card any cheaper. Instead, the retailer hands you a card as a bonus for buying something else. Walmart offered a $300 gift card with a qualifying iPhone 18 purchase for Black Friday, and Barnes & Noble gave a $10 card for every $100 in gift cards bought. A bonus card doesn't lower what you pay for the item itself. A discounted card trims your bill from the first dollar. A bonus card is only worth counting if you were already planning the purchase and know you'll spend the card. Otherwise it's a reason to spend more, not a saving. Settle the store, the card's price and what you'll buy with it before you buy the card. That's how a gift card actually puts you ahead.

Card-linked cash back cuts the cost of a shopping trip without changing anything in your cart. Banks and card issuers, through programs like Chase Offers, Amex Offers and Bank of America's BankAmeriDeals, run promotions with specific retailers that credit money back on purchases you'd make anyway. The reward comes out of spending you'd already planned, not a new purchase. It lowers the cost of money you're already spending, and it gives you no reason to spend more.

The catch is that it only covers certain stores, and you have to switch it on. Chase claims its offers come through partnerships with select merchants, and you need to activate an offer before you make the purchase for it to count. Offers are usually tied to one card, too, so you have to pay with that card. The store you're heading to may not have an offer at all. Checking your banking app before you leave tells you whether the trip will earn anything. That means the app comes out before the card does. Some tools can handle the activating for you. Savewise, a browser extension and app, says its Pro tier automatically activates offers from Chase, SimplyMiles and Rakuten. It also tries to activate Amex offers, though it recommends adding those by hand for guaranteed activation. If you're still shopping this weekend, a quick check in the app before you reach the register is all this kind of cash back asks of you.

According to recent reports, cash back is a bonus on a good price, never a reason to accept a bad one. Money coming back feels good, and that feeling can make it easy to skip the question of whether the price was worth paying in the first place. "If you're not getting a good price on your purchase, earning 3% back doesn't matter," Jason Stauffer, a senior reporter at CNBC Select, remarked. A refund of a few percent won't turn an overpriced item into a bargain.

The order to follow is simple: judge the price, activate the offer, then pay.

Recent findings suggest that before you pay any Black Friday price, you can find out whether other people think it's worth paying. Slickdeals is a community site where shoppers post the deals they find, and its millions of members vote and comment on each one. Those votes and comments decide which deals get featured. In effect, you get the judgment of people who have already looked hard at the same offer. Commenters will say so when a posted deal is weaker than it looks, and they often share discount codes that actually work. When an offer comes with a significant advertised saving, the comments under it can tell you more than the headline above it. Reading them takes a minute, and the time to do it is before you check out.

Recent findings suggest that two things in those comments are worth looking for. The first is whether the store advertising the deal is even the right place to buy, since commenters sometimes point to another retailer selling the same item for less. If you trust the first store that promotes an offer, you may pay more than someone who scrolled a few replies further. The second is whether the discount is as massive as the store claims. Commenters often mention what the item cost before, which tells you whether it's been this cheap already. With that history in hand, you can hold a dramatic "was" price up against what the item has actually sold for, instead of taking the store's word for it.

On some items, the cheapest version for sale this weekend is one another shopper already sent back. Returned and open-box goods can cost less than the same item upcoming at its Black Friday price. Amazon indicates shoppers saved more than 25% on average on items from Amazon Resale, its used and returned goods section, last year. Each item is inspected and graded before it's resold. "Like New" means it works perfectly but the packaging may be damaged. The grades step down through "Very Good" and "Good" to "Acceptable," which can mean scratches, dents or missing parts. Best Buy does something similar with open-box items. Its Geek Squad grades them Excellent, Good or Fair, and the price moves with the grade. That makes open-box a better fit for things you're keeping than for gifts, because a beat-up box doesn't matter when the item is for you. The real question isn't whether it costs less. It's whether you trust the grade behind the lower price.

According to recent reports, amazon handles so many returns that some checks slip through. "Because it's such a large operation, things are missed," Zoe Lu, general manager at Helium 10, told CNBC. Amazon's seller programs find new buyers or new homes for more than 300 million items a year. At that volume, a flawed return can land in the resale listings without anyone catching it, and a missed check leaves the risk with you. That risk is worth taking on something you can test the day it arrives, not on something you can't. Read the return terms, too. Both Amazon and Best Buy say open-box and Resale items fall under their regular return policies. Best Buy notes that many open-box items keep the manufacturer's warranty, but it's worth confirming for the specific item.

The new price you're comparing against can also creep up. Amazon's fee changes led 65% of sellers to raise prices in 2024, according to a SmartScout survey cited by CNBC. Some of the gap between a new item and a returned one may come from a higher new price rather than a real bargain on the open-box version. The comparison that counts is the open-box price against the lowest price for a new one anywhere.

A returned item belongs in your cart only when it's the cheapest way to get the thing, not just the cheapest version of it at one store.

Shopping through a cash-back portal adds a second saving on top of the sale price. Click through to a retailer from a site like Rakuten or TopCashback and you earn a percentage back after the Black Friday discount. But that rebate is only worth having on a price that's already the lowest you can find, and a juicy cash-back rate can steer you to the wrong store. Say a TV costs $399 at a store paying 5% back, about $20, while the same set is $299 somewhere else. The cheaper store wins before any money comes back at all. So find the lowest price first, then check whether a portal covers that store.

Industry observers note that cash back can't count as part of the price you pay this weekend, because you don't have it yet. Rakuten says online and in-store purchases show up first as "pending." They typically take three to 14 weeks to be confirmed, a buffer that covers returns, exchanges and other changes to your order. Even then, Rakuten pays out only four times a year, on Feb. 15, May 15, Aug. 15 and Nov. 15. Cash back has to be confirmed before a payment date to make that check, and you need at least $5 confirmed to get paid. Cash back from a Black Friday purchase may not reach you until spring. Until then, it's a balance sitting with the portal, not money in your account. Treat it as a bonus to bank if it demonstrates up, not a number to subtract from the price at the register.

Two shoppers standing side by side in the same aisle can pay different prices for the same item, depending on whether one of them is signed in. Plenty of retailers save some prices for members and app customers. Target Circle, Target's free loyalty program, gives members automatic deals and personalized offers in the Target app. So finding the lowest price this weekend depends on which store you're in and on what that store knows about you. The check takes seconds. Before you reach the register, open the store's app or sign in to your account and see whether it offers you a lower price than the one on the shelf. If it doesn't, you've lost a moment. If it does, the number on the tag was never the lowest price the store was willing to charge you.

A members' price is only cheaper once you count what it cost to become a member. Paying to join a program just to grab a small markdown is a bad trade, because you pay the fee before you see any discount. Paid tiers often sell themselves on early access rather than lower prices. Target Circle 360 members got 24 hours of early access to select Black Friday deals. Walmart+ members got Walmart's online "Hot Deal" drops a day before everyone else, and non-members could still buy them the next day while supplies lasted. That gives you a simple rule in the aisle. A free app or a free account passes the test, because access costs nothing and any lower price is a real saving. A paid membership taken out for one weekend of sales usually fails. The fee goes on the bill alongside whatever you buy, and on a modest purchase the discount may never earn it back.

The fee is part of the price, so add it in before you decide the members' rate is a bargain.

Recent findings suggest that A bundle looks like the easiest win in the store: one price covers the thing you came for plus a few extras. That single price is also what makes the deal hard to judge, because you can't see what any one piece costs. A bad bundle can cost you in two ways. Sometimes the package is only slightly cheaper than buying the parts on their own. Other times, part of what you pay goes to accessories you'll never use, which means spending money on things that were never on your list. A bundle only counts as a discount once you've shown that it is one.

Sources indicate that the test takes a few minutes on your phone in the aisle. Look up what each item in the bundle costs on its own and add up the prices. It's the one check that tells you whether the package is cheaper than buying just what you need. Keep the comparison like for like, with the same model, the same size and the same extras, because pricing a cheaper lookalike tells you nothing about the bundle on the shelf. The Federal Trade Commission's Guides Against Deceptive Pricing say a "was" price should be a real price the item was regularly offered at, not a number inflated to make a discount look bigger. A bundle's savings claim rests on a reference price too, and here that reference is what the parts cost separately. The difference is that you can look this one up on the spot instead of taking it on trust. If the parts add up to roughly the bundle price, buy only the item you came for and leave the extras behind.

Sources indicate that plenty of shoppers head into this weekend's sales already entitled to a lower price than the one on the tag, without thinking of it as a Black Friday tool. Student, military and teacher discounts can undercut the public sale price, and some go well past an ordinary markdown. HP's Education Program advertises up to 40% off for U.S. students, their parents and teachers. So before you chase the loudest sale sign, figure out which groups you belong to. The best price you can get may depend on who you are, not what day it is.

Recent findings suggest that A student or military rate doesn't win by default. Some are small enough that an ordinary sale beats them, and some take money off an add-on rather than the item itself. Nike's student discount is 10% off most items, and it can't be combined with other promo codes except free shipping. For a student shopping at Nike, any Black Friday markdown deeper than 10% is the better deal. Apple's education pricing includes up to 10% off AppleCare+ coverage for a new Mac or iPad, and a discount on a protection plan is hard to weigh against the price on the laptop's sale tag. Keep in mind that "up to" is a ceiling, so the rate on a given product can be smaller. The sensible move is to put your verified discount price next to the sale price and pay whichever is lower.

It has been revealed that A discount has to be proved before it counts, and for a last-minute shopper that proof is the step most likely to be missing. Many retailers run verification through third-party services. Apple uses UNiDAYS, and Nike uses SheerID, which can ask you to upload documents. Nike then emails a single-use code, which works only online, not in Nike stores. Military discounts follow a similar pattern. Nike gives active, reserve, veteran and retired service members 10% off, verified online through SheerID or with a military ID in U.S. stores. Many retailers offer similar rates to teachers, nurses and first responders, so check before assuming students are the only group with a deal.

It has been revealed that sort out your status on your phone before you get in line. At the register, the sale price is the only one on offer.

Recent findings suggest that this trick pays you for doing nothing at checkout. Fill an online cart, get as far as checkout, then leave without paying, and some retailers will email you a discount code to come back. To the store, an abandoned cart is a sale it wants back, and the code is its offer to win you over. On a weekend built around buying fast, the shopper who pauses can end up paying less than the one who clicks "buy" right away.

In a recent development, nothing about the reward is guaranteed, starting with whether it shows up at all. The tactic depends on the retailer having your email, so you need to be signed in or to have entered your address at checkout. Many retailers do send codes. Electronics retailers and marketplaces like Amazon rarely do, according to research by data firm Decodo reported by ConsumerAffairs. That rules out a lot of the major-ticket items people buy on Black Friday. The size of the discount varies just as much. Decodo found offers ranging from free shipping to as much as 65% off, with fast-fashion brands often sending 10% to 15% within about 12 hours. Waiting has costs of its own. Popular items can sell out, and a price can rise before the code arrives, so screenshot what you saw before you walk away.

According to recent reports, A free gift takes nothing off the bill, so it only counts as a saving if you actually want it. Even then, it's only a saving once you've checked that the main item costs no more than it does at other stores. Picture an offer of $100 in free accessories. If you wouldn't have paid even $10 for those accessories, the gift is worth almost nothing to you, whatever value the store puts on it.

Sources indicate that retailers hand out giveaways this week mainly to get people through the door. "Retailers need to offer an attractive incentive for shoppers to visit their store first," retail analyst Bruce Winder told TheStreet. Some of those incentives come down to luck. Michaels is giving away 500 "Countdown to Craftsmas" Advent calendars at each store starting on Black Friday, and only one calendar per store holds a $100 gift card. That's roughly a 1-in-500 shot. If you make the trip for that card, you'll most likely go home without it, after walking past the sale shelves the store wanted you to see.

Sources indicate that A freebie can get you in the door, but it doesn't decide whether the trip paid off. TheStreet reports that Neil Saunders, managing director of retail at GlobalData, expects shoppers to want a visit that was worth making, whatever stunt brought them there. Whether a visit was worth making comes down to the price of what you buy. Price the main item against other stores as if no gift came with it. If it costs less, the freebie is a genuine bonus. If it costs more, the gift saved you nothing.

A free gift is the easiest extra to mistake for a saving, because it makes you feel richer even when it saves you nothing.

If the people in the thread have shown that a deal is weaker than it looks, walk past it, however substantial the advertised saving.

If you always use the same portal out of habit, you could be leaving money on the table, because portals don't all pay the same rate at the same store. Cashback Monitor tracks the rates different portals pay at a given retailer, so you can see who's paying the most before you click. It also demonstrates how a store's best rate has moved over time, which helps you spot a holiday bump. Rates change often, and the gap matters most on massive-ticket purchases. That's exactly what a lot of Black Friday shoppers are buying, so any large purchase is worth a quick comparison.

Check the price, then check the portals, and treat whatever comes back as a pleasant surprise rather than part of the deal.

Extras are a way to get you to hand over more at the register, even when each piece looks like a deal.

The bigger risk is that the email talks you into finishing a purchase you'd abandoned for a good reason. Retailers send the code right after you've stopped short of paying, and that timing is what makes it so hard to ignore. A sudden 10% off is a nudge, not a reason. The code works best as a small bonus on something you'd already decided to buy, never as the reason to buy it.

Wait for a code only on things you would have paid full price for anyway, because a cart worth abandoning is still worth abandoning at 10% off.

Breaking: Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • In a recent development, the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

In a recent development, the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the firm acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the tech giant’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company indicates it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

Sources indicate that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software revision that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

In a recent development, so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

Sources indicate that the final report doesn’t say what the July enhancement was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report claims.

In a recent development, first, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

In a recent development, how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report indicates.

According to recent reports, the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Recent findings suggest that once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft states it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also aims to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

It has been revealed that some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

In a recent development, the report also confirms what Microsoft stated the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

The latest testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the manufacturer says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

Tech Report: Your Blueprint for Next Year Could Be in Trouble Before It Even Begins — Unless You Ask the Right Question

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three newly introduced priorities competing for specialist capacity.
  • Recent findings suggest that the planning baseline also indicated an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the newly introduced year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three newly introduced priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

Recent findings suggest that the planning baseline also indicated an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the newly introduced year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

In a recent development, during the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the upcoming priorities to start as planned. The program lead mentioned the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

Industry observers note that what the planning discussion didn’t do was force the remediation work to compete again with the three upcoming priorities. It sat in the baseline as committed work, while leaders debated how to allocate what they believed was the remaining capacity.

By the end of the session, the team had made disciplined choices:.

The overcommitment was already there.

Recent findings suggest that the problem became visible in the first weeks of execution. One of the approved priorities needed several of the same risk, legal and data specialists who were still closing the remediation program.

The planning model counted those people as partially available because the older work was expected to wind down early in the year. Instead, a final set of regulatory findings required more analysis, and a small group of specialists stayed fully engaged.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced priority still had its approved funding, executive sponsor and start date. The people needed to move it weren’t actually free.

The old work was visible, but its claim on the upcoming year’s capacity had been treated as fixed background rather than as a choice.

Managers began stretching the same specialists across both commitments. The new priority’s first milestone slipped as specialist reviews that should have happened early were pushed behind remediation work. Meetings multiplied, decisions slowed, and work that looked fully staffed on paper started moving in fragments.

The pressure spread beyond those specialists. Project leads started moving milestones to fit the people they could get, finance held back some spending because dependent work couldn’t start, and senior leaders spent more time resolving clashes between commitments they believed had already been reconciled during planning.

The interesting thing was that the approved blueprint hadn’t changed, but the amount of work that could move at the same time already had.

The upcoming initiative hadn’t been badly prioritized at all. The leadership team had already removed a lower-ranked proposal, but part of the capacity used in the ranking exercise simply hadn’t been available to begin with.

This is where the “Hidden Problems” execution leak appears.

The planning process had surfaced the remediation program, its budget and its expected completion date, yet the fresh work was still being ranked against an overstated view of what remained available.

A baseline records what’s already in motion, but it doesn’t force old work to justify its capacity against latest work. Once carryover is treated as given, only the new initiatives are asked to compete.

That distinction matters because visibility can create false confidence.

Leaders can see every major piece of work on one page and still never face the question of whether an old commitment deserves to keep the people and budget it carried across the year boundary.

Listing carryover isn’t the same as choosing it again. The planning process therefore becomes disciplined about one side of the load while leaving the other side untouched.

Recent findings suggest that when execution starts slowly, leadership tightens prioritization. Leaders ask for fewer initiatives, sharper business cases and clearer ranking, then delay or reject fresh proposals that can’t justify scarce capacity.

Those actions improve the choices among upcoming priorities; however, they don’t reopen the older commitments already sitting in the baseline. That was the pattern in this business unit.

Leadership had reduced the new-priority list before approving the initiative, and when capacity pressure appeared, the first response was to ask whether one of the new initiatives should move more slowly.

The remediation program wasn’t part of that debate because it had been approved in the prior year, and finishing it was treated as an “obligation” rather than as a competing use of scarce capacity.

The organization was re-ranking newly introduced work while the carryover never faced the same test.

It has been revealed that A stronger planning process adds a formal carryover line. That certainly improves visibility, but it doesn’t change the underlying mechanism when carryover remains exempt from comparison.

The remediation work can appear clearly in the plan, with its budget, owner and expected completion date, and still never face the one central question: Is finishing this work now more valuable than starting the fresh priority that needs the same people?

According to recent reports, in this business unit, the remediation program remained on every planning view. Its existence was never hidden. What did stay hidden was the effect of treating its capacity claim as “non-negotiable” while the newly introduced priorities competed for whatever was left.

The initiative could be complete as an inventory and incomplete as a capacity decision.

Every item appeared somewhere, but not every item had to earn its place in the same contest for scarce people and budget.

In a recent development, by the time the conflict became obvious, leaders were dealing with a problem the planning process had already created. The remediation work couldn’t simply stop, and the new priority had already been approved.

According to recent reports, the same scarce specialists now sat between two legitimate commitments, each with consequences for delay. Leaders were forced to make the tradeoff during execution instead of during planning, when they still had more room to change the portfolio.

When that conflict reached the next leadership review, the discussion was no longer about which work deserved to start. It was about which already-approved commitment would lose access to people both sides now depended on.

Recent findings suggest that the proposal didn’t fail because leaders chose the wrong new priorities. Not at all. The planning choice had been postponed until both commitments were already in motion.

In a recent development, A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three new priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

The planning baseline also showed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the latest year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

Sources indicate that during the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the new priorities to start as planned. Tech Report: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 latest articles.
  • “Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes.
  • I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 latest articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces.

Industry observers note that at Bergens Tidende, known as BT, reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one.

Vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he states the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most important point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way.

Office workers describe something different. In a Workday survey of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by researchers at BetterUp and Stanford, each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows.

Recent findings suggest that A Georgia Tech researcher argued this month that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking.

In a recent development, johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster.

Industry observers note that on one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson said. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less important.

A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice.

It has been revealed that so has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published.

I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025 master’s thesis at Aalto University made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.”.

Recent findings suggest that for companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable.

As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • According to recent reports, under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

It has been revealed that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app indicates the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

According to recent reports, under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

In a recent development, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

Industry observers note that the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

In a recent development, for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

It has been revealed that for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Recent findings suggest that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Industry observers note that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks demonstrates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

According to recent reports, the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

Recent findings suggest that the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Industry observers note that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Recent findings suggest that the bonus was simple.
  • In a recent development, after it started, creative quality dropped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

In a recent development, after it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

Sources indicate that the target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the blueprint asked for.

I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

According to recent reports, for a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

We traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

When we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. Upcoming editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

That changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

It has been revealed that A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

Bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

We stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

Recent findings suggest that the results came promptly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

The difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

We’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

The early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

Recent findings suggest that while the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Sources indicate that before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

Sources indicate that if you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

Industry observers note that after it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

Recent findings suggest that the target noted completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those highlights up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the blueprint asked for.
