#156456. Buy now, pay later on Black Friday: 7 checks before you split a payment

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2992 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Buy now, pay later on Black Friday: 7 checks before you split a payment

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Using buy now, pay later on Black Friday can make holiday deals easier to manage, but fees, due dates, returns and credit checks deserve a look first.
  • A split payment changes when you pay for something, not what you owe for it.
  • It has been revealed that black Friday is the day after U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Using buy now, pay later on Black Friday can make holiday deals easier to manage, but fees, due dates, returns and credit checks deserve a look first.

A split payment changes when you pay for something, not what you owe for it. That distinction is easy to lose at checkout, where a pay-in-four button can make a large purchase look like a small one.

It has been revealed that black Friday is the day after U.S. Thanksgiving, which falls on the fourth Thursday of November. It opens a stretch of holiday shopping that runs straight into December bills. Retailers promote deals with short deadlines, and checkout pages often list installment plans alongside cards and digital wallets. Providers such as Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm and PayPal $PYPL appear at checkout on many retail sites, and some stores offer their own versions.

The basic model works like this. A pay-in-four plan divides a purchase into four equal payments. The first is due when you check out. The rest are collected on a set schedule, usually by automatic charge to a linked card. Longer intends stretch payments over months and can carry interest. Each provider writes its own terms, and those terms can change.

That variation is the reason to slow down before using buy now, pay later on Black Friday. Two prepares that look identical on a product page can still differ. They may treat missed payments, returns and credit reporting in different ways. The answers sit in the provider's app and disclosures, not in the retailer's banner ad.

According to recent reports, the checks below are meant to be done before you tap the button, not after the confirmation email arrives. They start with the total amount you will repay and how it compares with the sticker price. They move through late-fee rules, the timing of each installment against your paydays and the card that will be charged. They also cover how refunds work when an item goes back and how providers handle credit checks and reporting. The last covers how to keep track of several aims running at once.

Industry observers note that each check answers a specific question about a specific plan. The result is a checkout decision made with the full terms in view, rather than one made under the pressure of a sale clock.

Before agreeing to a buy now, pay later plan, compare the total you will repay with the sticker price of the item. If the two figures match, the plan changes only when you pay. If the total is higher, the difference is what the borrowing costs.

Industry observers note that on a pay-in-four plan, the four installments together should equal the checkout price. If they add up to more, find out what the extra covers before confirming.

Longer aims can work differently. Monthly installment loans from providers such as Affirm can carry interest. Once interest applies, the payments added together can exceed the price on the tag. At the same rate, a loan that runs longer gives interest more time to build.

According to recent reports, rates differ by provider and by shopper. Two people buying the same television from the same retailer may be offered different terms. A rate seen on a friend's blueprint, or on an earlier purchase, says little about the offer on the screen today.

Recent findings suggest that the check itself is simple arithmetic. Find the installment amount and the number of payments on the strategy summary shown before you confirm. Multiply the installment amount by the number of payments. Then set that figure beside the full checkout price, including tax and shipping. If the multiplied figure is larger, the gap is the price of spreading the cost out.

In a recent development, check the number of payments as closely as the amount. A proposal with a smaller installment may simply run for more months. A lower monthly figure does not mean a lower total.

The comparison carries extra weight on discounted items. Black Friday sales are built around markdowns. Interest charged on a sale item eats into the discount. Depending on the rate and the length of the loan, it can shrink the saving or erase it. The fair comparison is the sale price paid outright, not the original price the retailer crossed out.

When the total repaid exceeds the sticker price, the shopper has a clear choice. One path is to accept that extra cost knowingly. The other is to pay a different way.

Industry observers note that know what a buy now, pay later provider does when an installment is missed before you split a Black Friday purchase. Klarna and Afterpay may charge late fees. Affirm has remarked it does not charge late fees.

In a recent development, A shopper who picks one of these providers at checkout is also picking the rules for the weeks after the sale. The missed-payment rules come from the provider's agreement with the shopper.

Fee policies can change. A provider can revise its terms. The version that applied to a purchase last year may not match the one in force this Black Friday. The reference that counts is the current agreement shown in the provider's app or disclosures at the time of purchase.

Industry observers note that the word "may" in a fee summary matters too. Whether a fee applies to a specific order is set out in the current terms, not in a general description of the provider.

Reading that agreement means looking for a few specific answers. Does the provider charge anything for a missed installment? If it does, is the charge a flat amount or tied to the size of the order? Does the agreement set a limit on total fees for a single purchase?

Timing is the next thing to look for. Check whether the terms describe a window after a missed due date before any fee applies. Check whether the provider tries the charge again, and when. See whether a due date can be moved before it arrives.

Industry observers note that A fee is not the only rule worth knowing. Look for what a missed payment means for using the same provider on later orders. The same app may appear at checkout again before the holiday shopping season ends.

Affirm's statement covers late fees only. It does not describe everything else in its agreement. The rest of its terms still need a full read.

Industry observers note that A screenshot of the fee section taken at checkout creates a record of the rules shown when you agreed. That record helps if a question about a charge comes up weeks later. Keep it with the order confirmation.

It has been revealed that before splitting a Black Friday purchase, match each installment's due date to the day money actually lands in your account. The first payment comes out at checkout. The rest follow a schedule the provider sets, not one built around your pay cycle.

It has been revealed that many providers collect the remaining three installments about every two weeks. That pattern is common, but it is not universal. Schedules vary by provider. The exact dates appear at checkout and in the provider's app, and those are the dates that count.

Industry observers note that on a two-week rhythm, the last payment lands roughly six weeks after the purchase. Black Friday falls in late November. A blueprint opened that day would run into early January.

That window matters because of what else sits inside it. December brings regular monthly bills, and often more holiday spending on top of them. A split payment taken on Black Friday adds three more draws across the same weeks. Putting them on a calendar before checkout makes the overlap visible.

It has been revealed that the practical step is to write down your income dates for the next six weeks. Then place each installment date beside them. If an installment falls a day or two before a paycheck arrives, that payment has to come from money already in the account. If it falls just after payday, it competes with rent, utilities and other fixed costs due around the same time.

The first installment deserves separate attention. It is charged on Black Friday itself, whatever your pay schedule. A shopper paid at the end of the month may be near the bottom of the cycle when that charge hits.

Someone paid every two weeks may find the installments line up closely with paydays. Someone paid once a month may see most installments fall between paychecks. Neither pattern rules out a strategy on its own. What matters is knowing which one applies before agreeing to the terms.

Do not assume a due date can be moved later. If a provider offers any way to change one, its terms will spell that out. Read them before relying on that option.

Industry observers note that the card linked to a buy now, pay later proposal determines what a short balance will cost. A debit card exposes the shopper to bank overdraft or declined-payment fees, while a credit card adds its own interest on any balance carried.

Installments on split-payment plans are usually charged automatically to the card the shopper links at checkout. Each later payment comes off that card on its due date, with no further action needed. The card chosen during a Black Friday checkout shapes what happens on every one of those dates.

According to recent reports, A debit card draws directly on a bank account. The money leaves the account on the day the installment is collected, not the day the item was bought. If the balance is short on that day, the bank may cover the charge and apply an overdraft fee. It may instead refuse the charge and apply a declined-payment fee.

In a recent development, those bank charges sit apart from the BNPL initiative itself. A refused charge can also leave the installment unpaid. That brings the provider's own missed-payment rules into play. Reading both the bank's fee terms and the provider's terms covers each side of that risk.

It has been revealed that the practical risk with debit funding is timing inside the account. Rent, utilities, subscriptions and other automatic debits may draw on the same balance in the same week. An installment that looked small at checkout can be the charge that pushes the account below zero.

A credit card moves the installments off the bank account, but it does not remove cost. Each installment joins the card's balance. If the shopper carries part of that balance from month to month, the card's interest applies to it.

That means a initiative with no interest of its own can still end up costing interest. The card issuer charges that interest, not the BNPL provider. The card also has its own payment date, separate from the installment schedule.

Before confirming a split payment, a shopper can check which card the proposal will charge and what that card's terms say about carried balances. For a debit card, the useful question is whether the linked account will hold enough on each collection date, not only on Black Friday itself.

It has been revealed that A refund on a buy now, pay later purchase goes through the BNPL provider, not only the retailer. Installments may keep coming due until the return is processed. Read the store's return policy and the provider's refund process before you check out.

It has been revealed that A split payment creates two separate relationships. The retailer decides whether an item can come back and how long you have to send it. The provider manages the loan, including how a refund is applied to your initiative.

Industry observers note that start with the retailer. Find the return window for the specific item you are buying. Check whether the product page or receipt marks it as final sale or lists different conditions for discounted stock. Black Friday markdowns deserve this extra look before you commit.

Then turn to the provider. Its refund process explains what happens to an installment plan once the retailer accepts a return. Look for it in the provider's app or help pages before you agree to the plan, not after a package is already in transit.

In a recent development, the weak point is the gap between sending an item back and the refund posting. A return has to be shipped, received and processed by the retailer. Until that happens, scheduled payments may still be charged to your linked card. Budget for them as though you had kept the item.

In a recent development, keep a simple paper trail for every split purchase you might return. That means the order confirmation, any return authorization, the shipping receipt and the tracking number. If a refund stalls, those records show when the item left your hands.

Sources indicate that if a refund never arrives, or the retailer and provider give different answers, the next step is the provider's own dispute policy. Rules for disputing BNPL purchases in the U.S. have been subject to regulatory change. Do not assume a specific federal protection covers your purchase. Read the provider's current dispute terms, which set out how to raise a problem and what the provider will review.

It has been revealed that gifts bought on an installment proposal need one more check. The plan belongs to the buyer, even if someone else sends the item back. Ask the recipient to tell you when they return it, then watch your plan for the adjustment.

It has been revealed that buy now, pay later providers differ on two credit questions: the type of credit check run at approval and whether the loan is reported to credit bureaus. Check both in the provider's disclosures before splitting a Black Friday purchase. One app's answer does not carry over to another.

The first question is about approval. Some buy now, pay later providers run a soft credit check when a shopper applies. Others run a hard credit check. The provider decides which one applies, and its own terms are the place to confirm it.

The second question is about what happens after approval. Some providers report their installment loans to credit bureaus, and some do not. That choice decides whether a blueprint appears on a shopper's credit file at all.

The two answers are independent. A provider can handle its approval check one way and its bureau reporting another. Each question needs its own look in the disclosures.

The practical step is to open the provider's app or website before checkout. Find the sections that cover credit checks and credit reporting. A sale-day checkout screen may show only the payment amounts. The credit details may sit somewhere else entirely.

Sources indicate that when a retailer offers more than one split-payment option, the comparison can include these two points alongside the payment terms. Noting each provider's approach to checks and reporting keeps the options straight. That record also helps when the same shopper sees different providers at different stores over the holiday weekend.

There is no single answer to whether buy now, pay later hurts credit. The question has to be asked plan by plan. Reading that provider's disclosures is the reliable way to know what a specific plan involves.

It has been revealed that if a provider's disclosures leave either question unanswered, that gap is something to weigh before agreeing to split the payment. The same check applies to any store-specific plan offered at checkout during Black Friday sales.

Industry observers note that before adding a fresh buy now, pay later plan during Black Friday sales, list every plan already running, with its next due date and remaining balance. That single tally shows what you already owe before another installment joins the queue.

It has been revealed that split payments are easy to stack. A shopper can hold plans with Klarna, Afterpay, Affirm and PayPal $PYPL at the same time, plus a store-specific option from a single retailer. Each plan runs on its own autopay date. None of them waits for the others.

According to recent reports, that separation makes the total hard to see. Each provider's app indicates the intends held with that provider. It does not show a pay-in-four proposal opened elsewhere a week earlier. A shopper checking one app sees only part of what is owed.

Industry observers note that the tally itself needs only three columns. The first names the provider and the item bought. The second records the next due date. The third records the balance still owed on that plan. A notes app, a spreadsheet or a sheet of paper all work.

Recent findings suggest that fill it in by opening each provider's app or account in turn. Copy the dates and balances directly from those screens rather than from memory. Include store-specific prepares. They are easy to miss because they sit inside a retailer's own checkout or account.

Industry observers note that once the list is complete, add up the third column. That sum is the amount still due across every active plan. Then sort the rows by due date. The sorted list reveals which days carry more than one payment and how closely the charges bunch together.

According to recent reports, only then look at the fresh purchase. Add it as a fresh row, with its own first payment and its own future dates. Compare the new total with the old one. If the new row lands on a date that already holds other payments, that clustering is visible before checkout rather than after.

Keep the list current through the rest of the holiday season. Looks opened over the Black Friday weekend can still be collecting payments well into December. Update a row each time a payment clears, and delete it when the balance reaches zero. A plan that is dropped from the list too early, or never added, leaves the total incomplete.

Industry News: Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the tech giant-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

In a recent development, marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis remarked the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis remarked.

Sources indicate that since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making fresh data centers harder to build. The manufacturer cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders stated. A second, larger site using AMD’s newly introduced Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The manufacturer states it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Sources indicate that srinivasan said that at the massive tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Industry observers note that competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

Recent findings suggest that coreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Sources indicate that marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

It has been revealed that much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders stated. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Recent findings suggest that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe aims to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis remarked. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking tech giant DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Sources indicate that angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Recent findings suggest that past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis noted the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one significant customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis stated he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of fresh chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

According to recent reports, updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Inflation remains stubborn. Producer prices are now running at a 6.5% annual clip, and affordability is top of mind. Want to cut some costs in your business? Of course you do. Try these moves.

Recent findings suggest that both ChatGPT and Claude offer connections to your bank account and credit card services. Or, if you’re nervous about that, just upload your statements. You’ll be impressed by the number of suggestions they make to reduce your spending and better manage expenses.

Sources indicate that I used to think canceling online subscriptions would be a big headache, and years ago it was. Not anymore. Search for “cancel my subscription on Google Play” (or Apple or Amazon), and you’ll get direct links to do it. I’m betting you and your business have subscriptions you’ve forgotten about that are eating up hundreds of dollars a year.

It has been revealed that every year, put your business and auto insurance policies out for a quote. Ask your AI chatbot to make suggestions too. This is not very time-consuming and can be accomplished using an administrative person in your office. We’re oftentimes too lazy to do this. And that’s costing us.

It has been revealed that many of my clients have complicated, expensive coffee machines in their break rooms with a wide variety of coffees. They also stock sugar packets, teas, mini creamers, plastic stirrers and paper cups. It’s too much. Offer fewer coffees so you order less. Put out a sugar bowl, bring in a gallon of creamer and go back to ceramic mugs. Call me Scrooge, but it saves money.

In a recent development, nerdWallet does a great job regularly reviewing business and personal credit cards. Again, use your AI chatbot to look at your spending and tell it your preferences and you’ll get plenty of recommendations too. Moving to a better card could earn you more points and cashback rewards then you’re getting right now. I have some clients that regularly switch back and forth.

Speaking of credit, if your business buys products on Amazon, then make sure you use one of Amazon’s credit cards for purchases. With a Prime membership, you can earn 5% back on eligible Amazon purchases, and there’s no annual fee.

If you can’t pay off a credit card purchase right away from operations, consider using working capital or a lower-rate loan to reduce the balance. Credit card interest rates are high, so this can cut what you pay in interest significantly.

Industry observers note that this is a very common tax move, yet so many of us ignore it. Put as much as you can into your retirement proposal to lower your tax bill this year. When you save – assuming you’re eligible – sock money into a Roth IRA or Roth 401K so your after-tax money grows tax-free. With a Roth, there are no minimum distributions, and you can take the money out whenever you want, provided it meets certain requirements like a first-time home purchase, higher education or unreimbursed medical expenses.

Make sure your manufacturer has an HSA and contribute the max. It will reduce your tax expense and allow you to save money for future healthcare expenses.

In a recent development, every square foot your inventory takes up costs you in overhead and space. Twice a year, take a hard look at your inventory and get rid of what isn’t moving. Sell it on Craigslist, eBay or Facebook Marketplace or scrap it.

Mark Cuban’s Cost Plus Drugs and Amazon Pharmacy both offer options that let businesses provide discounted prescription drugs, and they work with many popular health aims.

Set up a donor-advised fund and contribute to it this year, even if you haven’t decided which charities or nonprofits will receive the money. You take the deduction now and choose the recipients later.

Sources indicate that I like Capital One Shopping. Add it as a browser extension for yourself and anyone else who makes purchases for your business. Whenever someone is on a shopping site, it searches for available coupons before you buy. It works about half the time, and it has saved me significant money over the years.

Sources indicate that we can all afford the things we want — it’s just that sometimes we choose to spend our money on other things instead. That’s fine. But know that cutting back on things like travel, entertainment, subscriptions, marketing or other discretionary spending in your business (and your personal life) can help you reallocate your cash for other purposes. You’re more in control than you think.

#156453. AI boom or bust? 10 under-the-radar stock picks and investing ideas for either scenario

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1373 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

AI boom or bust? 10 under-the-radar stock picks and investing ideas for either scenario

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1373 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Investors don’t have to decide whether AI will change the world.
  • The same goes if the bubble bursts—a risk that Nvidia’s recent troubles heighten.
  • Industry observers note that to help navigate both sides of the trade, Fortune has identified six investment strategies for 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Investors don’t have to decide whether AI will change the world. They do, however, have to determine how much of their portfolio should depend on it. After all, AI bets now extend far beyond the obvious megacap tech stocks. Utilities and power-equipment makers have been swept up in the data center build-out. Even parts of the energy sector now trade on the promise that AI will consume an enormous amount of electricity.

The same goes if the bubble bursts—a risk that Nvidia’s recent troubles heighten. Because classic AI stocks are weighted so heavily in indexes like the S&P 500, even a standard 60/40 portfolio can mean betting major on this nascent technology. Investors looking to hedge must find something that doesn’t depend on the very boom they’re worried about.

Industry observers note that to help navigate both sides of the trade, Fortune has identified six investment strategies for 2027. Three are built to ride the boom—and three will help you survive a bust.

The VanEck Data Center Supply Chain ETF allocates to companies that help power, operate, and equip data centers. It’s a bet on the physical infrastructure of the AI boom rather than solely the hyperscalers and software developers themselves.

Industry observers note that that’s because the fund gives investors exposure to several layers of the data center supply chain. Think chipmakers, along with companies that make important computing components, like Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, and Micron. Industrial companies like Eaton, Vertiv, and Johnson Controls that provide the electrical equipment and cooling solutions for these energy-intensive facilities are included as well. Meanwhile, Quanta Services and Amphenol add exposure to the construction and connectivity themes.

Tom Essaye, founder of Sevens Report Research, likened the broadening AI trade to “water sweeping across a floor,” reaching “places that people would not think had anything to do with AI.”.

Bryan Armour, director of ETF and passive strategies research for North America at Morningstar, points to RACK as a way to look beyond traditional tech funds and growth stocks to capitalize on the AI trade. “You need to build the data centers, you need to build the chips and the GPUs and memory and all the different components,” Armour said.

The Roundhill Neocloud ETF bets on the landlords of AI computing: businesses that build specialized data centers packed with GPUs and rent out the processing power AI companies need to train and run their models.

Recent findings suggest that two neocloud providers, Nebius and CoreWeave, make up more than half of the fund; many of the rest have been in Bitcoin mining and are retooling for AI. The bet is that rising demand for computing will fill up these facilities and lead to new contracts.

Industry observers note that the Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (LYTE) and the KraneShares Photonic and Optical ETF (LUMA) both target a key bottleneck in the AI build-out: moving enormous amounts of data promptly and efficiently. Both funds offer exposure to companies developing optical technologies that increase bandwidth and reduce the energy needed to move information between chips and across data centers as AI computing demands grow.

Recent findings suggest that these ETFs invest in the suppliers behind those connections. LYTE holds stocks such as Ciena and Eoptolink, while KraneShares’ LUMA counts LandMark Optoelectronics, Soitec, and Marvell among its major holdings.

“AI will still have legs next year,” remarked Todd Rosenbluth, head of research at VettaFi. “There will still be demand for companies that offer [this] exposure.”.

Still, investors allocating to these more specialized funds must be prepared: All the names here launched in 2026, so they don’t have long track records and tend to swoon when the AI trade comes under pressure. “The narrower you invest in the market,” Rosenbluth said, “the greater the volatility.”.

Recent findings suggest that think the AI boom is overheated? These strategies can help hedge your portfolio if the AI trade falls back to earth.

Industry observers note that the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF offers a straightforward way to loosen AI’s grip on your portfolio. Unlike the traditional S&P 500 index, which gives the biggest companies the largest weighting, RSP resets its holdings to equal weighting each quarter. That puts chipmaking giant Nvidia on par with any other company at each quarterly rebalance. If megacap tech underperforms while the rest of the market holds up, RSP could lose less than the traditional S&P 500 index. That stated, for the first nine months of 2026, RSP returned roughly 9.9%, including reinvested dividends, lagging the broad-market index’s 12.7% total return.

The Invesco S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) buys the 100 S&P 500 stocks with the smallest price swings over the previous 12 months. SPLV can offset some AI risk because the fund allocates to seemingly steadier businesses, rather than companies with exceptionally high growth expectations. The fund has little exposure to Massive Tech and much larger allocations to utilities, financials, and real estate. Because SPLV counts utilities among its holdings, however, it’s not completely AI-free.

Although SPLV lagged the S&P 500 during the first nine months of 2026, it remained positive for the year through Sept. 30. The fund provided some downside cushioning in 2022, when the Federal Reserve started aggressively hiking interest rates. That year, in total returns, the S&P 500 dropped 18.1%, while SPLV fell only 4.9%.

Recent findings suggest that the iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV) targets high-paying dividend stocks. The appeal is less “this manufacturer could change the world” and more “this company can pay shareholders now.” Investors who want a stake in established businesses rather than expectations of explosive growth might consider HDV. It’s been a banner year for the fund, with a strong first nine months in 2026. Including reinvested dividends, HDV returned approximately 17.5%, beating the S&P 500’s total return of 12.75%.

Recent findings suggest that the strategy is not foolproof, though. Companies can cut their dividends, and the fund can dive with the broader market; however, it can be a different and welcome source of returns.

According to recent reports, the Vanguard Morningstar Value ETF (VTV) invests in large-cap stocks that are considered relatively inexpensive against their business fundamentals. Where the AI trade often asks investors to pay up for future growth, value investing means finding assets that are trading for less than their intrinsic worth. That makes VTV a potential hedge if the market sours on these growth stocks.

Industry observers note that JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil, and Johnson & Johnson are among the fund’s holdings, as well as a smattering of tech names like Micron. For the first nine months of 2026, VTV returned approximately 14.8%.

Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities offer a hedge against a less obvious risk of the AI boom: that building the future makes everything more expensive. A massive build-out of data centers, power plants, and transmission lines could weigh on supplies of equipment and skilled labor. That can push inflation higher.

Industry observers note that these government bonds adjust their principal with the consumer price index. Their fixed interest rate applies to that adjusted balance, meaning payments rise alongside inflation. Investors can access TIPS through funds such as the Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF (VTIP) and the iShares TIPS Bond ETF (TIP). Although both lagged the S&P 500 during the first nine months of 2026, when inflation was rampant they held up much better. (In 2022, on a total return basis, including distributions, the S&P 500 tumbled more than 18%, while VTIP and TIP shed roughly 3% and 12%, respectively.).

VettaFi’s Rosenbluth warns that inflation is not in the rearview mirror, in his opinion. “The environment we’re in today, where companies are spending a lot to support artificial intelligence, that can and has been contributing to inflation being elevated.”.

For Rosenbluth, that concern fits into a broader challenge for 2027, when some view this breakthrough technology as overhyped and others believe it’s still in the early stages. Making sure a portfolio has room for more than one outcome is key.

“Everyone is long AI,” he mentioned. The priority is “just having a balanced portfolio, because there’s just such a wide range of potential outcomes next year.”.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 glitch of Fortune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor sees newly introduced ways to put Bitcoin (BTC) to work on Wall Street.

Industry observers note that according to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S. derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses.

‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov. 23.

As per the guidance, these companies must maintain sufficient financial resources to cover their operating costs for at least a year.

As clarified by CFTC staff, Bitcoin and Ether can be used to meet this requirement (as well as payment stablecoins). The advisory also provides guidance on how staff interpret the current rules. It also applies to swap execution facilities (SEFs), which are platforms where counterparties trade swaps.

Industry observers note that bitcoin holdings worth $10 million could count for $8 million toward the annual requirement, based on the minimum 20% discount that CFTC staff stated they would accept. This provides some flexibility in case Bitcoin's price falls. The discount is also called a haircut.

Industry observers note that for Ether, the same minimum 20% haircut applies. For payment stablecoins, the haircut is 2%.

This provides some incentive for an exchange to actually hold BTC. Exchanges could hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets and use some of its value to satisfy this reserve requirement. There would be no need to sell it for USD first.

Sources indicate that however, a futures exchange still needs to have sufficient unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities to cover its operating costs for at least six months. Bitcoin, Ether and even payment stablecoins do not fall into this category.

Industry observers note that the same six-month liquidity requirement applies to clearinghouses. Additionally, they need to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover a default by a clearing member.

It has been revealed that CFTC staff also noted a potential downside for exchanges holding crypto reserves. During a market slump, there's a risk that an exchange's operating losses might rise. At the same time, the value of the Bitcoin it holds to cover those losses might fall.

So this possibility should be considered before an exchange decides whether to use Bitcoin to meet its financial resource requirements.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It notes: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

In a recent development, the schedule is fixed. Circle confirmed in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide claims "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Industry observers note that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide states "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

In a recent development, the migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

The main text above it indicates something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

It has been revealed that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

Sources indicate that tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the tech giant started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

Sources indicate that the key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

In a recent development, that personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Sources indicate that then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

According to recent reports, tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk stated the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

Sources indicate that you don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:.

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold.

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if people join the network.

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

In a recent development, and the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S.
  • Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith noted the president is “making an crucial point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith noted the president is “making an crucial point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he mentioned most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from Latest Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he stated.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Recent findings suggest that his one example was an unnamed manufacturer that wants to build in Finland. Google unveiled a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, stated he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a substantial technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, noted Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the tech giant for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate manufacturer, and noted Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith noted Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

In a recent development, he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

#156448. Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1133 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Industry observers note that when a organization confirms layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first.
  • AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a tech giant needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that when a organization confirms layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a tech giant needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

Recent findings suggest that that distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people swiftly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

Industry observers note that there is another way to implement AI. Start by asking how it can make your people more capable.

Recent findings suggest that I learned this lesson long before the current AI boom. When we were building Amazon Web Services, talented engineers were spending too much time provisioning servers, configuring storage and handling infrastructure before they could get to the work they were actually there to do. By removing that friction, we gave developers more capacity to build, experiment and solve customer problems.

Industry observers note that I saw the same principle years later with a junior attorney who spent hours researching and formatting before reaching the work that required her judgment. Generative AI could produce a first draft in minutes, giving her more time to refine the facts and shape the narrative for the client’s best outcome.

That is the opportunity leaders should look for with AI. Before calculating how many positions an efficiency gain could eliminate, ask what your people could accomplish if repetitive work stopped consuming so much of their day.

Suppose AI gives a team back 10 or 20% of its capacity. What happens to that time?

It could be the customer follow-up that keeps getting postponed, an improvement sitting in the backlog or a relationship that needs more attention. Those opportunities already exist inside most businesses. The problem is that people have been too busy with repetitive work to pursue them.

I saw this with a team of customer service agents who spent a significant portion of their day filling out forms and navigating cumbersome systems. An AI tool automated part of that process and gave them roughly an hour back each day.

Leadership could have used that hour to justify a smaller team. Instead, employees spent more time connecting with customers, strengthening relationships and solving more complex problems. AI removed work they disliked and created room for work where they could contribute more.

Retaining talent requires planning for people at the beginning of an AI initiative rather than after deployment. If leaders automate first and ask what happens to employees later, the priority is already clear.

In a recent development, before introducing AI, divide the work into three categories. Some tasks contain little meaningful judgment and can be automated. Others can be accelerated by AI while still requiring human judgment. A third group should remain primarily human because relationships, creativity or judgment create the value. Then make the next decision before deploying anything. Where will the recovered capacity go?

Sources indicate that that could mean moving people toward customer relationships, product development, higher-level analysis or other work that contributes more directly to growth. The destination will vary by organization, but leaders should know where they want people to go before technology begins changing their roles.

How you introduce AI also shapes whether employees embrace or resist it. If the first message people hear is that a tool will save 40% of their time, they may immediately wonder what leadership plans to do with that 40%.

In a recent development, tell employees which frustrating work you want to reduce. Show them what they will have more time to accomplish. Explain how their roles can become more valuable as AI handles repetitive tasks.

Then demonstrate that commitment through what happens next. If employees see recovered time consistently reinvested into better work, stronger skills and fresh opportunities, AI starts to look like a tool they can use rather than a threat they need to survive.

In a recent development, leaders can begin before buying another AI tool. Take one team and map how AI could change its work, then answer these four questions together before deployment.

In a recent development, 1. What work should disappear? Break roles into individual tasks and identify repetitive work that consumes time without requiring significant human judgment. Focus first on removing friction rather than removing positions.

2. What human capability should grow? For every task AI can automate or accelerate, identify what employees could do with the recovered time. Look for work involving customers, relationships, creativity, problem-solving or judgment.

3. Where will the recovered capacity go? Give those hours a destination before deployment. If AI saves a team eight hours each week, decide whether those hours will go toward customer service, innovation, upcoming revenue opportunities or another measurable priority.

4. What will you tell employees? Explain what AI will take off their plates and what you want them doing more of as a result. Managers should be able to describe that future clearly before asking employees to adopt the technology.

According to recent reports, AI will change jobs, and some roles will change significantly as companies redesign how work gets done. But leaders still control a critical decision about what they do with the capacity AI creates.

It has been revealed that before treating efficiency as a reason to reduce headcount, ask what your people could accomplish with the time they get back. The companies that answer that question first have an opportunity to use AI for something far more valuable than cutting costs. They can use it to build a more capable workforce.

Recent findings suggest that when a tech giant announces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a organization needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

Recent findings suggest that that distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

Each account trading on the XRP Ledger's decentralized exchange moved an average of 4,328 XRP a day in the third quarter of 2026, up 437% from 805 XRP in the same quarter a year earlier, according to a report that XRP treasury tech giant Evernorth released on Tuesday.

According to recent reports, according to Evernorth, the average swap on the XRP Ledger reached 35 XRP in the third quarter, up from 19 XRP in the second quarter and under 6 XRP a year earlier. "The growth came from bigger trades, not more of them," the organization wrote in the report.

At the same time, the number of accounts trading on the XRP Ledger's order book fell to 1,042 a day in the third quarter of 2026 from 2,027 a day in the third quarter of 2025. The number stood at 1,203 in the fourth quarter of 2025, 1,324 in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,125 in the second quarter, according to the report.

Order-book volume on the XRP Ledger rose to 4.51 million XRP a day in the third quarter from 1.63 million XRP a day a year earlier, Evernorth data indicates.

In total, 5.16 million XRP a day was traded on the XRP Ledger's exchange in the third quarter, and the figure was up 96% year over year, according to Evernorth.

According to recent reports, measured in U.S. dollars, exchange volume on the XRP Ledger fell 15% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the report.

Evernorth also compared the XRP Ledger with Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche and Polygon. Across these seven networks, exchange volume in dollars fell 42% over the same period, the report highlights.

XRP was trading at around $0.93 on Tuesday morning after reaching as high as $1.026 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap.

In a recent development, the report also shows that the average balance of Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin on the XRP Ledger reached $937 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from $539 million in the second quarter. By the end of the quarter, the RLUSD balance on the XRP Ledger stood at $1.15 billion, compared with $670 million at the end of the second quarter, and the number of RLUSD holders on the network rose to 67,449 from 45,620.

According to Evernorth, the XRP Ledger's average share of RLUSD reached 48.5% in the third quarter, up from 34% in the second quarter. Still, Ethereum finished the quarter with more RLUSD than the XRP Ledger. Evernorth noted that on Ethereum, RLUSD "can already be lent," and that on the XRP Ledger, "native lending is in validator voting.".

Sources indicate that as of Nov. 20, the Lending Protocol amendment had 24 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. The amendment needs 29 votes, held for 14 days, to activate.

Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9, and its shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN on Oct. 12. The company entered the public markets holding approximately 473 million XRP, according to its press release.

Evernorth announced the deal in October 2025, with investments from SBI, Ripple, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Since Grant Canary launched his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary launched his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a upcoming line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Sources indicate that just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

It has been revealed that humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the concerns.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

Recent findings suggest that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

Sources indicate that that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

According to recent reports, my personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally important: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Fresh York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

In a recent development, nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

It has been revealed that my hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

Industry News: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback.
  • It has been revealed that I read it differently.
  • Recent findings suggest that on November 12, Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored.

It has been revealed that I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every firm whose CEO looks irreplaceable.

The sequence of events tells a story.

Recent findings suggest that on November 12, Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates.

Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.”.

Sources indicate that then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government. Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision.

In a recent development, the board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished.

That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that states no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options.

A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.

Recent findings suggest that accountability depends on a credible alternative. When a board has a successor ready, its questions carry weight, because everyone in the room knows the organization survives if the answers fall short. When it has nobody, the CEO holds the leverage and both sides know it. The duty to oversee him turns into a duty to keep him.

Sources indicate that huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. The board had three decades to prepare for the day he wasn’t there. When that day came, it had a CFO doing two jobs, one outside name, and a market that wanted him back. Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld wrote in Fortune the board had no Plan B.

According to recent reports, investors made the same point from the other side. Within days of the resignation, prominent shareholders were urging the board to keep the door open to Huang. Nobody outside the manufacturer had the facts. What they were pricing was a business with no one else to run it.

Industry observers note that the board has since created a national security committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Those are controls on conduct. Neither one is a successor.

Industry observers note that I coach CEOs, and I’ve watched how boards arrive here. Nobody decides to skip succession. It gets postponed, one good quarter at a time.

Industry observers note that over the years a founder’s identity and the tech giant’s fuse. Raising the question of who comes next starts to feel like disloyalty, so directors leave it for another meeting. The CEO rarely pushes either. Planning your own exit means picturing a company that no longer needs you, and that is the hardest thing to ask of someone whose whole identity is the company.

Industry observers note that so both sides stay comfortable. The cost arrives on the one day the board needs a choice and finds it doesn’t have one.

Plenty of boards are living with the same arrangement right now, and it’s invisible for as long as the results are good.

Two tests will tell a director where their board stands.

According to recent reports, first, name the person who could run the manufacturer on Monday. One name, already inside the building, whom the top team would follow. If the honest answer is the CFO as caretaker, you have a holding pattern.

Second, recall the last time the board said no to the CEO on something he cared about. If nobody can remember one, the board has already stopped overseeing him. It just hasn’t been tested yet.

According to recent reports, huang may prove to be the right leader for Nvidia’s next chapter. The investigation may answer every open question. Neither would change what the 11 days showed.

The board now enters the next crisis in a weaker position than the last one. It has shown its investors, its government and its CEO that it has no alternative to him. He knows it. So does everyone who will ever need to challenge him.

Every director reading this should ask the question Nvidia’s board had to answer in public.

If our CEO were gone tomorrow, would we have a choice?
